Infectious disease follows an infectious cause such as tuberculosis, which nothing here suggests. Rehabilitation after her prolonged illness is the need.
Genetic evaluation is not indicated for her pericardial disease. She needs rehabilitation.

opts: Synchronized shocks need a consistent QRS and a pulse. Pulseless polymorphic tachycardia is defibrillated.
ruled out by a stated finding
Magnesium breaks torsades in a conscious patient; a pulseless patient needs defibrillation first.
Pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms. A pulseless polymorphic tachycardia is defibrillated.

opts: Correct. Peripheral neuropathy, common in older patients with diabetes or alcoholism, causes a continuous burning sensation in the foot that is unaffected by exercise, unlike arterial claudication.
Ischemic rest pain is worse with elevation and relieved by dangling the leg, and pulses are diminished. Her pulses are normal and position has no effect.
Spinal stenosis gives claudication-like pain with walking, relieved by sitting or leaning forward. Burning that is constant and unaffected by exercise is neuropathy.
Arterial claudication is activity-related pain relieved by rest, with diminished pulses below the lesion. Constant burning unaffected by exercise with normal pulses is neuropathy.

ruled out by a stated finding

A.q: A 60-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy has orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat), crackles at both lung bases and diminished breath sounds at the right base. A chest radiograph is ordered. Which finding on the film would indicate pulmonary edema?
opts: A normal film that excludes congestion
The radiograph in dilated cardiomyopathy is expected to show cardiomegaly and effusions, and edema may show as Kerley B lines. A normal film would not fit his crackles.
Short horizontal lines meeting the pleura

Correct. Kerley B lines are horizontal lines 1 to 2 cm long that meet the pleura at right angles and indicate pulmonary edema. Cardiomegaly and pleural effusions are the other expected radiograph findings.
A small heart with clear lung fields
Dilated cardiomyopathy shows cardiomegaly, pleural effusions and pulmonary edema on the chest radiograph. A small heart with clear lungs would argue against congestion.
Pericardial thickening is the imaging clue to constrictive pericarditis, and it is shown on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging rather than as the sign of pulmonary edema.

A.q: Which electrocardiogram changes occur in Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: Left bundle branch block is the conduction delay described in dilated cardiomyopathy.
Low QRS voltage in all leads
Low QRS voltage suggests amyloid infiltration in restrictive cardiomyopathy, not stress cardiomyopathy.
ST elevation and T wave inversion
Correct. The electrocardiogram shows ST segment elevation and T wave inversion, which is why the syndrome is managed like acute coronary syndrome until catheterization.
Prominent inferior and lateral Q waves reflect septal hypertrophy in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

A.q: A 72-year-old woman has sudden chest pain and diaphoresis an hour after learning she has lost her savings in a financial collapse. The electrocardiogram shows ST elevation and troponin is elevated. No catheterization has been done yet. Which is the most appropriate initial approach?
opts: An emotional trigger does not exclude an acute coronary syndrome, and there are no reliable early features to tell them apart. She is managed on coronary protocols.

Correct. Stress cardiomyopathy mimics acute coronary syndrome, and because there are no reliable early differences, evaluation and treatment follow the established protocols for acute coronary syndrome patients.
Nothing in her presentation calls for an inotrope. With no reliable early differences from a coronary event, she follows acute coronary syndrome protocols.
Alcohol septal ablation treats outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. ST elevation with chest pain is managed on acute coronary syndrome protocols.

A.q: A 66-year-old man with stable cardiomyopathy on full medical therapy says he tires after walking a block and feels anxious about exercising. He has no symptoms at rest. Which referral is most appropriate to improve his exercise tolerance?
opts: Hospice referral is for end-stage cardiomyopathy. A stable patient with limited exercise tolerance is referred to cardiac rehabilitation instead.
Competitive sport is not the goal for a patient who tires after a block. Structured cardiac rehabilitation builds exercise tolerance and quality of life.
Genetic screening targets hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in adolescents and families with inherited disease. It would not improve his own exercise tolerance.

Correct. Cardiac rehabilitation programs improve exercise tolerance and quality of life, with education on medication adherence, nutrition and symptom monitoring, and psychological support for chronic illness.

A.q: Which is the first treatment for torsades de pointes in a conscious patient?
opts: Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Intravenous magnesium is the first treatment.
Amiodarone prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Intravenous magnesium is the first treatment.
Beta blockers are avoided in torsades because the slower rate lengthens the QT. Magnesium is given first.

A.q: What is the most frequent presumed cause of myocarditis in developed countries?
opts: Correct. In developed countries viral infection is presumed to be the most frequent cause, including parvovirus B19, enteroviruses such as Coxsackie group B, adenoviruses and hepatitis C.
Lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and myasthenia gravis are causes, but the most frequent presumed cause in developed countries is viral infection.
Penicillin, thiazide diuretics, tetracycline and methyldopa can cause myocarditis, but viral infection is presumed most frequent.
Bacteria such as diphtheria, meningococcus and Mycoplasma can cause myocarditis, but viral infection is presumed most frequent in developed countries.

A.q: A 78-year-old man with recurrent urinary tract infections has aortic valve endocarditis, and his blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Nafcillin plus rifampin belongs to staphylococcal prosthetic valve therapy, not enterococcal disease.
Cefazolin is a methicillin-susceptible staphylococcal option, not an enterococcal regimen.
A single oral amoxicillin dose is dental prophylaxis, not treatment of established endocarditis.
Correct. Enterococcal endocarditis is treated with ampicillin (or penicillin G) plus gentamicin, ampicillin plus ceftriaxone, or vancomycin plus gentamicin.

A.q: Erythema extending well beyond the margin of an inflamed vein raises suspicion of which condition?
opts: Correct. When erythema extends significantly beyond the margin of the vein, septic thrombophlebitis should be suspected; simple thrombophlebitis keeps its redness along the vein's course.
Simple superficial phlebitis produces erythema that follows the vein. Redness spreading far beyond the vein margin suggests infection within the vein, or septic thrombophlebitis.
Lipodermatosclerosis is long-standing firm, scarred skin and fat at the medial ankle. Acute redness spreading beyond a vein's margin suggests septic thrombophlebitis.
Stasis dermatitis is a chronic eczematous rash of the lower legs from venous insufficiency. Redness spreading beyond one inflamed vein points to septic thrombophlebitis.

A.q: What must follow chest or back pain in a patient with a known thoracic aortic aneurysm?
opts: Correct. Chest or back pain with a known or suspected thoracic aortic aneurysm must undergo urgent imaging to rule out the aneurysm as the cause of the pain.
Pain changes the urgency. It requires urgent imaging, not routine scheduled surveillance.
Pain cannot be dismissed. Urgent imaging must rule out the aneurysm as its cause.

A.q: A 49-year-old man has 3 weeks of fever and night sweats. Two separate blood cultures grow Streptococcus gallolyticus, and a transesophageal echocardiogram shows an oscillating mass on the aortic valve. He has no skin, eye or kidney findings. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Possible is one major plus one minor, or three minor criteria. He has two major criteria, which is definite.
No further test is needed to classify him; two major criteria already make the diagnosis definite.
Two separate cultures of a typical organism and an oscillating mass are two major criteria, which confirm endocarditis rather than exclude it.

Correct. Two major criteria are met: a typical organism (Streptococcus gallolyticus) in two separate cultures and an oscillating mass on echocardiogram. Two major criteria alone establish definite endocarditis.

A.q: A 19-year-old swimmer has an electrocardiogram before a sports physical. She has no symptoms. The rate is 72, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS, but the beats come closer together as she breathes in and spread apart as she breathes out. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A normal P wave before every narrow QRS at 60 to 100, with the rate rising on inspiration and falling on expiration, is sinus arrhythmia: a normal, physiologic rhythm that is irregular with a pattern.
Sick sinus syndrome produces pauses, sinus arrest or tachy-brady swings in a diseased node, usually with symptoms; a breathing-linked variation in a healthy swimmer is sinus arrhythmia.
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves; she has a normal P wave before every beat and a regular pattern tied to breathing.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a fast, irregular rhythm with at least three P-wave shapes in acutely ill lung or heart patients; her single P-wave shape at 72 is sinus.

A.q: A 29-year-old woman has superficial thrombophlebitis of the forearm after an intravenous catheter and asks whether the clot can travel to her lungs. Which statement about her outlook is accurate?
opts: Pulmonary embolism is the usual outcome
Pulmonary embolism is the feared complication of deep vein thrombosis. Superficial thrombophlebitis rarely embolizes, so this outcome is the exception rather than the rule.

Correct. Superficial phlebitis and thrombophlebitis rarely cause serious complications and rarely embolize, which distinguishes them from deep vein thrombosis, where pulmonary embolism is the major complication.
Chronic venous insufficiency follows in most
Chronic venous insufficiency is a late result of deep vein thrombosis that scars the valves. It is not the expected outcome of an uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis.
Fatal embolism is likely without treatment
Even untreated deep vein thrombosis carries a small rate of fatal embolism. A superficial clot rarely embolizes at all, so a fatal event is not expected.

A.q: A 32-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and outflow tract obstruction has breathlessness and chest tightness on exertion. His blood pressure is 124/78 and heart rate is 76. He takes no cardiac medication yet. Which is the initial medication for his outflow obstruction?
opts: Diuretics lower preload and can worsen obstruction; if needed they are used with caution to avoid dehydration. The initial drug for obstruction is a beta blocker.
A beta blocker such as metoprolol

Correct. A beta blocker such as metoprolol is the initial medication for left ventricular outflow tract obstruction; it slows the heart and improves diastolic filling. Verapamil or diltiazem is the alternative.
Nitrates reduce preload and afterload, which aggravates outflow tract obstruction, so they are avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A beta blocker comes first.
A positive inotrope such as digoxin
Positive inotropes such as digoxin increase contractility, raise the risk of ischemia and may induce arrhythmias, so they are avoided. A beta blocker is the initial drug.

A.q: A 36-year-old man has a regular tachycardia at 170 with an identical, abnormally shaped P wave before every QRS. Adenosine briefly slows the ventricular response, but the abnormal atrial rhythm continues unchanged afterward. Which rhythm does this response point to?
opts: Nodal reentry depends on the atrioventricular node and almost always terminates with adenosine; it also has hidden P waves.
ruled out by a stated finding
Orthodromic reentry uses the atrioventricular node and usually stops with adenosine; it shows a retrograde P wave after the QRS, not an abnormal P before it.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Adenosine is usually less effective at terminating focal atrial tachycardia than nodal or accessory pathway reentry, so persistence of an abnormal-P-wave rhythm after adenosine is the diagnostic clue.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with at least three P-wave shapes; an identical abnormal P wave before every QRS in a regular rhythm comes from a single focus.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.q: A 78-year-old man with no neurologic symptoms has a 90% carotid stenosis on duplex. He has advanced cancer, and his expected survival is about two years. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Repeating the scan does not change the missing criterion, a life expectancy over five years. His asymptomatic stenosis is managed medically.
The stenosis exceeds 80%, but asymptomatic surgery also requires a life expectancy of more than five years. With about two years, medical management is advised.

Correct. Surgery for an asymptomatic stenosis is advised only above 80% together with a life expectancy over five years. His limited survival means medical therapy: antiplatelets, risk-factor control and smoking cessation.
Stenting still counts as surgical revascularization and carries the same asymptomatic criteria, including life expectancy over five years. He should be managed medically.

A.q: A 29-year-old woman who delivered a healthy baby three months ago now has breathlessness on exertion, orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat) and swollen ankles. She had no heart disease before pregnancy. Echocardiogram shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an inherited thickening of the septum with a small cavity and a normal ejection fraction. A dilated ventricle three months postpartum fits peripartum disease.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy has stiff walls, a near-normal cavity and big atria, often after radiation or infiltrative disease. A newly dilated, weak ventricle after delivery is peripartum cardiomyopathy.
Correct. Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a rare form of dilated cardiomyopathy that develops in the last trimester of pregnancy or within the first six months after delivery, as it has here.

Stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy follows an emotional or physical stressor, mostly in postmenopausal women, and causes transient mid and apical hypokinesis rather than a dilated ventricle after pregnancy.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
A.q: A 19-year-old college athlete has exertional chest pain without coronary disease and a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border. Hypertension and aortic valve disease have been excluded. Which echocardiogram finding confirms the clinical diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Pericardial thickening marks constrictive pericarditis and is shown on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. The hypertrophic diagnosis rests on unexplained wall thickening.
Unexplained wall of 1.5 cm or more

Correct. The clinical diagnosis is confirmed when echocardiography shows unexplained left ventricular wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more anywhere in the wall, most often as asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a small cavity.
Dilated thin walls with low fraction
Dilated, thin walls with a reduced ejection fraction describe dilated cardiomyopathy. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has thick walls, a small cavity and a normal or high ejection fraction.
Mid and apical hypokinesis after a stressor is stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is confirmed by an unexplained wall of 1.5 cm or more.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: A 48-year-old man becomes hypotensive and short of breath an hour after a catheter procedure perforates his heart. Echocardiogram shows only a small pericardial effusion, estimated at about 150 mL, with right ventricular diastolic collapse. Which best explains why so little fluid has compromised him?
opts: Rapid filling of an unstretched sac
Correct. Acute effusions can produce tamponade with small amounts of fluid (under 200 mL) because the pericardium has no time to stretch, unlike chronic effusions that grow large over time.
A pericardium that stretches over time lets a chronic effusion grow large without tamponade; here the fluid arrived fast into an unstretched sac, so under 200 mL was enough.
Calcification belongs to constriction. Here the problem is rapid fluid entry into a normal, unstretched sac.
There is no need to assume a measurement error; small, rapid effusions can cause tamponade.

A.q: A 58-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for colon cancer comes to the emergency department with three days of left calf swelling that measures 4 cm more than the right, plus tenderness along the deep veins of the calf. He has no history of clots and nothing else explains his leg. The team debates whether to order a D-dimer or go straight to imaging. Using the Wells criteria, which is the best next step?
opts: Correct. Active cancer, calf swelling over 3 cm and tenderness along the deep veins total 3 points, a high likelihood. A score of 3 or more skips the D-dimer and goes directly to venous duplex ultrasound of the leg.
The ankle-brachial index screens for peripheral artery disease in arterial insufficiency. His swollen, tender calf points to venous thrombosis, so the test needed is venous duplex ultrasound.
Contrast ascending venography is the invasive gold standard but has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound, which is noninvasive and is the imaging test ordered for a high score.
Starting with a D-dimer is the low likelihood path. With a high Wells score the D-dimer is skipped, because even a negative result would not exclude deep vein thrombosis and ultrasound is needed.

A.q: A 31-year-old man was treated for acute pericarditis 3 months ago and has been symptom-free for 6 weeks. His sharp, positional chest pain has now returned with a friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound). C-reactive protein is mildly raised. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Anti-interleukin-1 therapy is for colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent recurrence with a strong inflammatory phenotype, not a first recurrence.
Prednisone alone is not the recurrence regimen; when used it is given with colchicine. Anti-inflammatory plus colchicine for 6 months or more comes first.
Ibuprofen with colchicine, stopped at 2 weeks
Two weeks of colchicine is far too short after a recurrence; the course is 6 months or more.
Ibuprofen with colchicine for 6 months or more

Correct. This is a first recurrence, symptoms returning after a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer, treated with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug plus colchicine for 6 months or more.

A.q: A 37-year-old man with acute pericarditis feels better after 5 days of ibuprofen and colchicine and plans to stop both medicines now. Which counseling point is most important?
opts: Switch to prednisone to finish faster
Prednisone is second line and does not shorten the course. Completing the prescribed regimen prevents recurrence.
Stopping now is safe since the pain is gone
Pain relief at 5 days does not mean the inflammation has resolved; stopping early raises the risk of recurrence.
Finish the full course to prevent recurrence
Correct. Patient education stresses adherence to the full treatment course to prevent recurrence, which affects about 15 to 30% of patients, together with activity restriction and red-flag symptoms.
Colchicine can stop; keep the ibuprofen
Colchicine is continued for about 3 months after a first episode because it reduces recurrence; it should not be dropped early.

A.q: A 39-year-old woman with visible varicose veins asks what symptoms she is most likely to have. Which should she be told?
opts: Sharp pain at rest when lying flat
Rest pain that worsens when the leg is raised is a feature of critical arterial ischemia. Varicose veins cause dull heaviness that builds with standing.
Correct. The most common symptom of varicose veins is a dull, achy heaviness or fatigue brought on by periods of standing, sometimes with itching over the veins.
Numbness and burning describe neuropathy. Varicose veins produce aching heaviness and fatigue with standing and may itch over the veins.
Calf cramping that eases with rest
Cramping on walking that resolves with rest is claudication from arterial disease. Varicose vein symptoms come on with standing.

A.q: A 72-year-old man with a known abdominal aortic aneurysm reports early satiety and pain isolated to his right groin, with no abdominal tenderness. Which explains the groin pain?
opts: Renal colic is a misdiagnosis of aneurysm pain, not its explanation. Isolated groin pain here is from the aneurysm pressing on the femoral nerve.
A femoral pseudoaneurysm follows catheterization with local swelling. With a known aortic aneurysm, isolated groin pain reflects femoral nerve pressure.
Correct. A symptomatic unruptured aneurysm can cause isolated groin pain from pressure on the femoral nerve, alongside abdominal, back or flank pain and early satiety as it expands.
A hernia is not among the aneurysm's described symptoms. Isolated groin pain in a symptomatic aneurysm comes from pressure on the femoral nerve.

A.q: A slow sinus rhythm that is causing hypotension and confusion is treated first with which drug?
opts: Metoprolol is a beta blocker, and beta blockers are a listed cause of sinus bradycardia; giving one would worsen the problem.
Digoxin is a listed drug cause of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, so it would slow the heart further rather than rescue it.
Correct. Acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia is treated first with atropine, then a temporary pacemaker if it fails; chronic symptomatic disease needs a permanent pacemaker.
Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node to stop supraventricular tachycardia; in a slow, unstable rhythm it would deepen the bradycardia.

A.q: A 2-month-old infant with a central line has poor feeding, fast breathing, tachycardia and a changing murmur. Blood cultures are positive and echocardiography shows a vegetation. Which complications are particularly common in infants because of septic emboli?
opts: Classic peripheral stigmata are considerably less common in children; infants' septic emboli cause osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia.
Glomerulonephritis is an immunologic sign, not the listed infant complication of septic emboli.
Pediatric endocarditis causes less heart failure than adult disease; septic emboli are the infant problem.
Correct. Septic emboli are common in neonates and infants, producing osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia, and neurologic signs such as seizures, hemiparesis and apnea.

A.q: A 60-year-old woman has viridans streptococcal endocarditis diagnosed early, before any heart failure or abscess, and she starts appropriate antibiotics the same day. Which statement about her outlook is most accurate?
opts: Correct. Viridans streptococcal endocarditis has a relatively good prognosis if antibiotic treatment starts before complications occur.
A 30-40% valve replacement rate is described for enterococcal endocarditis, not early-treated viridans streptococci.
Highest mortality belongs to Staphylococcus aureus, especially on prosthetic valves.
Death within weeks describes untreated acute endocarditis, not early-treated viridans streptococcal disease.

A.q: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation at 170 has a blood pressure of 74/40 and is drowsy and confused. Which is the most appropriate immediate step?
opts: Oral rate control suits a stable patient without rapid ventricular response, not someone hypotensive and confused.
Three weeks of anticoagulation precedes elective outpatient cardioversion; instability needs cardioversion now.
Correct. Hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation (hypotension and altered mental status) is treated with synchronized cardioversion.
Intravenous rate control is for the stable patient with rapid ventricular response; this patient is unstable.

A.q: A 75-year-old man with complete heart block is stabilized with transcutaneous pacing in the emergency department. Which is the definitive treatment?
opts: An implantable cardioverter defibrillator shocks lethal ventricular rhythms. Complete block needs a permanent pacemaker.
Ablation destroys conduction tissue and is itself a named cause of complete block. The definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.
Correct. Transcutaneous pacing is the emergent bridge; the definitive treatment for complete (third-degree) atrioventricular block is a permanent pacemaker.
A beta blocker slows conduction further. Complete block is treated definitively with a permanent pacemaker.

A.q: A 66-year-old woman with chronic obstructive lung disease is admitted with an exacerbation. She is confused, and the monitor shows runs of skipped beats from frequent early, wide QRS complexes without P waves. Her arterial oxygen tension is low. Which underlying problem should be corrected first?
opts: Correct. Hypoxemia is a main cause of premature ventricular contractions, along with electrolyte imbalance, so her low oxygen should be corrected first.
Blood glucose is not a named trigger. Her low oxygen tension is the cause to correct first.
Blood pressure is not the named trigger. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance are the main causes of premature ventricular contractions.
Temperature is not the named trigger. Hypoxemia, with electrolyte imbalance, drives premature ventricular contractions.

A.q: In sick sinus syndrome, a fast run that is irregularly irregular with no P waves alternates with pauses. Which rhythm is the fast run?
opts: Correct. An irregularly irregular fast rhythm with no P waves is atrial fibrillation, and in tachy-brady syndrome, the form of sick sinus syndrome in which fast and slow rhythms alternate, atrial fibrillation is the most common tachyarrhythmia.

Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm in a few patients, who then need a pacemaker with a defibrillator, but it is regular and wide; an irregularly irregular run without P waves is atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding
Sinus tachycardia is regular, with a normal P wave before every QRS; in tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm comes from outside the failing sinus node, most commonly atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular too, but every QRS has a P wave, in at least three shapes; a fast run with no P waves is atrial fibrillation, the usual fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.q: A 78-year-old man with diabetes and known black, shriveled toe tips now has a moist, swollen, blistered forefoot. His temperature is 39.2 C and heart rate 118. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. Wet gangrene (moist, edematous, blistering tissue with bacterial infection, often clostridial) is a surgical emergency because of the risk of sepsis, unlike the dry gangrene common in peripheral artery disease.
Antiplatelet therapy treats chronic arterial disease and cannot control infected tissue. Wet gangrene with signs of sepsis needs emergency surgical care.
Waiting for demarcation suits dry gangrene, which is hard, dry and clearly demarcated. Wet gangrene with fever carries a risk of sepsis and is a surgical emergency.
Exercise therapy is for stable claudication. A moist, blistered, infected foot with fever and tachycardia is wet gangrene, a surgical emergency.

A.q: A 71-year-old man has been on strict bed rest for six days during an admission for pneumonia and now has swelling and aching of the entire left leg. Which component of the Virchow triad does his prolonged bed rest represent?
opts: Endothelial trauma is direct injury to the vein wall from surgery, fracture, burns, catheters or injection. Bed rest for pneumonia does not injure the vessel lining; it slows flow, which is stasis.
Arterial vasospasm is not a component of the Virchow triad, which comprises venous stasis, hypercoagulable state and endothelial trauma. Immobility acts on the veins by slowing their blood flow.

A hypercoagulable state is an inherited or acquired clotting tendency, such as factor V Leiden, cancer, estrogen use or pregnancy. Lying still changes blood flow rather than clotting chemistry, so it is stasis.

Correct. Bed rest is immobilization, which alters blood flow and lets blood pool in the leg veins, the venous stasis component of the Virchow triad. Prolonged immobilization raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis about twenty-fold.

A.q: Compared with Mobitz type I, Mobitz type II block carries a higher risk of which outcome?
opts: Atrial fibrillation is not the feared progression. Mobitz type II tends to progress to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death.
Mobitz type II does not regress into the more benign Mobitz type I. Its risk is progression to complete heart block and sudden death.
Sinus tachycardia is not a complication of Mobitz type II. The danger is progression to complete heart block with a weak escape rhythm.
Correct. Mobitz type II has a higher risk of progression to complete (third-degree) heart block and sudden cardiac death, which is why it is treated even without symptoms.

A.q: A 57-year-old woman with a moderate pericardial effusion was stable yesterday. Today her blood pressure is 96/64, her jugular venous pressure is elevated, and she has new sinus tachycardia at 128. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. In tamponade, sinus tachycardia may indicate significant hemodynamic compromise and is an indication for immediate pericardiocentesis, with fluid support until it is done.
Waiting a week ignores signs of significant compromise; immediate pericardiocentesis is indicated.
Diuretics reduce preload and would worsen tamponade. She needs immediate pericardiocentesis.
Rate control with a beta blocker
Her tachycardia compensates for a falling stroke volume; slowing it would drop cardiac output. She needs drainage.

A.q: A 66-year-old woman has a painful ulcer above the medial malleolus with a clean base, fibrinous exudate and serous drainage, surrounded by brown pigmentation and pitting edema. Her pedal pulses are strong and her ankle-brachial index is 1.10. Which measure is essential for the ulcer to heal?
opts: The ulcer has a clean base and no sign of infection. Without controlling edema and applying compression, a venous ulcer will not heal whatever dressing is used.
Valvuloplasty is occasionally successful and carries a high risk of postoperative deep vein thrombosis. Initial nonoperative care with compression comes first.
Flavonoids increase venous tone, but at most they are an add-on to compression and cannot replace it. Healing depends on compression and edema control.
Correct. Venous ulcers will not heal unless edema is controlled and compression is applied, and an ankle-brachial index of 1.10 shows compression is safe. Wound care referral supports this.

A.q: A 59-year-old woman had a left leg deep vein thrombosis 11 months ago. She now has chronic left leg heaviness, edema and brownish ankle skin that worsen with standing and improve with elevation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Post-thrombotic (postphlebitic) syndrome is symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency that follows a deep vein thrombosis, appearing 6 to 24 months later, with heaviness, edema and brownish skin change from venous hypertension.
Drug-induced edema, such as from dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, is usually bilateral without inflammation. Her unilateral swelling after a leg clot points to post-thrombotic syndrome.

Lymphedema is chronic swelling that usually follows pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation, and brownish hemosiderin staining is rare in it. Her prior leg clot, brown ankle skin and heaviness that eases with elevation point to a venous cause.
A recurrent clot would usually present acutely with new swelling, pain and warmth. Slowly progressive heaviness with skin change, relieved by elevation, points to chronic venous disease.

A.q: A 72-year-old woman with a femoral pseudoaneurysm after catheterization reports increasing thigh pain and tingling around the swelling. Which explains her pain?
opts: Ischemic rest pain is forefoot pain relieved by dependency in chronic disease. Groin-to-thigh pain here reflects swelling and nerve compression.
Correct. A pseudoaneurysm presents with pain from increased pressure due to swelling or from nerve compression by the expanding blood-filled cavity.
Retroperitoneal bleeding is the picture of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm with shock. Her local pain comes from swelling and nerve compression.
Atheroemboli cause painful blue toes, not pain around a groin swelling. Pseudoaneurysm pain is from swelling pressure or nerve compression.

A.q: A 66-year-old man has a story strongly suggesting constrictive pericarditis: edema, ascites, an elevated jugular venous pressure with the Kussmaul sign (a rise on inspiration). His chest radiograph shows no pericardial calcification. How should this radiograph be interpreted?
opts: Most patients with constriction show no calcification, so a clear radiograph cannot exclude it.
A film without calcium does not point to restrictive cardiomyopathy; that distinction relies on echocardiography, natriuretic peptide and imaging.
It shows the cause is tamponade
Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis of fluid under pressure; a radiograph without calcium says nothing in its favor.
Correct. Pericardial calcification is highly consistent with constriction when present, but most patients do not have it on chest radiograph, so a film without calcium cannot rule the diagnosis out.

A.q: A 22-year-old woman with a known accessory pathway has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 210, with a retrograde P wave (inverted) just after each QRS and no delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke). Which rhythm is most likely?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with three or more P-wave shapes before the QRS; hers is regular with a retrograde P after each QRS.
Antidromic reentry conducts down the accessory pathway, so the QRS is wide with a delta wave.
ruled out by a stated finding
Ventricular tachycardia is a wide complex rhythm arising below the bundle of His; hers is a narrow complex tachycardia.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Orthodromic atrioventricular reentry, the more common form, conducts down the node and back up the accessory pathway: a regular narrow tachycardia with no delta wave and a retrograde P wave after the QRS.

A.q: A 45-year-old woman has 2 months of fever, weight loss and fatigue. A new murmur with a tumor plop (a low-pitched early diastolic sound) is heard, and three sets of blood cultures drawn before any antibiotics are negative. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Atrial myxoma mimics endocarditis with fever and a new murmur, a tumor plop or mid-diastolic rumble, but it is a tumor and the cultures stay negative.
Lyme disease causes fever and, rarely, myocarditis; it does not produce a tumor plop.
Polymyalgia rheumatica causes myalgia and raised inflammatory markers, not a new murmur with a tumor plop.
Subacute endocarditis usually grows an organism in cultures drawn before antibiotics, and a tumor plop is the sign of a cardiac tumor.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.q: A 45-year-old man has a heart rate of 122 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. His temperature is 39.2°C and he has a productive cough and crackles at the right base. He is alert with a blood pressure of 126/78. Which is the best treatment for his heart rate?
opts: Vagal maneuvers are first line for reentrant supraventricular tachycardia; a fever-driven sinus tachycardia settles when the infection is treated.
Cardioversion is for unstable reentrant or fibrillatory rhythms; this stable sinus tachycardia needs its cause treated.
Correct. A sinus tachycardia from fever and infection is an appropriate response to a pathologic process, and appropriate sinus tachycardia is managed by treating the underlying cause.
Adenosine stops reentrant supraventricular tachycardia through the atrioventricular node; it has no role in a sinus tachycardia from fever.

A.q: A 66-year-old woman has had six days of worsening left leg pain and coolness. The limb has no sensory loss or weakness, and imaging shows an arterial thrombus. Which intervention fits this time frame?
opts: Exercise therapy is for chronic claudication. A new arterial thrombus under 14 days old is treated with catheter-directed thrombolysis.
Major amputation is reserved for irreversibly ischemic limbs with profound sensory loss and paralysis. Her viable limb within 14 days suits catheter-directed thrombolysis.
Aspirin is chronic antiplatelet therapy and will not dissolve an acute thrombus. Ischemia of under 14 days is an indication for catheter-directed thrombolysis.
Correct. Intra-arterial catheter-directed thrombolysis, with alteplase as the thrombolytic, is indicated for acute limb ischemia of less than 14 days' duration.

A.q: Which cardiac condition is listed among the risk factors for infective endocarditis?
opts: Stable angina reflects coronary disease, not a substrate for endocarditis. Congenital heart disease is one of the listed risk factors.
Sinus bradycardia is a rhythm, not a structural substrate for infection. Congenital heart disease is a listed risk factor.
Correct. Congenital heart disease is a listed risk factor, along with rheumatic heart disease, degenerative valve disease, intracardiac devices, prosthetic valves and injection drug use.
Elevated office blood pressure does not damage the endocardium. Congenital heart disease is the listed cardiac risk factor.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: Which definition fits cardiac tamponade?
opts: Inflammation of the sac lasting under four weeks
Inflammation of the pericardial sac lasting less than 4 to 6 weeks is acute pericarditis. Tamponade is defined by fluid under pressure compressing the heart.
Fibrous scarring that leaves the pericardium inelastic
Fibrous scarring with loss of elasticity of the pericardial sac, making it noncompliant, defines constrictive pericarditis, the other compressive syndrome.
Pericardial fluid under pressure compressing the heart
Correct. Cardiac tamponade is an accumulation of pericardial fluid under pressure, resulting in compression of the heart; it is one of the pericardial compressive syndromes.
Extra pericardial fluid with no hemodynamic effect
Extra fluid in the pericardial space without major hemodynamic compromise is a simple pericardial effusion. Tamponade needs that fluid to be under pressure and compressing the heart.

A.q: A 71-year-old woman with suspected endocarditis has a urinalysis sent as part of her workup. Which urinalysis result is most consistent with endocarditis?
opts: Glucose and ketones point to diabetes, not endocarditis, whose urinalysis shows hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria.
Urine bilirubin and urobilinogen point to liver or hemolytic disease, not endocarditis.
Correct. Urinalysis in endocarditis can show hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria, reflecting renal involvement such as glomerulonephritis or emboli.
Nitrites without cells is not the pattern; hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria are.

A.q: A 73-year-old man with painful blue toes and palpable pulses asks what the emboli in his toes are made of. Which answer is accurate?
opts: A clot from the heart is a thromboembolus, the usual cause of acute limb ischemia with absent pulses. Blue toes with pulses reflect cholesterol-rich debris from plaque.
Correct. Atheroembolism is multiple small deposits of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris embolizing from proximal atherosclerotic lesions to the small vessels of skin and muscle.
Air embolism is not the process described. Atheroemboli are small deposits of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from proximal plaques.
Valve vegetations are not the source named for blue toe syndrome. The debris is fibrin, platelets and cholesterol shed from proximal atherosclerotic plaques.

opts: Adenosine does not prepare a patient for cardioversion; three weeks of anticoagulation does.
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms and is not a prerequisite for cardioversion; 21 days of anticoagulation is.
Correct. Outpatient cardioversion of atrial flutter is done after 21 days of anticoagulation, and anticoagulation is part of flutter management.
Ablation is the definitive alternative to cardioversion, not a step before it; anticoagulation comes first.

A.q: A 34-year-old woman has an electrocardiogram before a sports tryout. The QRS is 0.14 seconds, with an rsR' pattern (a small upward wave, a dip, then a taller second upward wave) in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in leads I and aVL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: An accessory pathway gives a short PR and a slurred QRS upstroke (a delta wave), not rsR' in the right precordial leads.
Ventricular tachycardia is a fast wide rhythm without P waves. A routine tracing with rsR' in V1 is right bundle branch block.
Left bundle branch block gives a dominant S wave in V1 and absent Q waves in the lateral leads, not rsR' in V1.
Correct. A QRS over 0.12 seconds with rsR' (bunny ears) in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in I and aVL is right bundle branch block.

A.q: A 66-year-old man is readmitted 3 weeks after coronary artery bypass surgery with fever, pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) chest pain eased by sitting forward, and a friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound). His sternal wound looks clean. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Constriction is a later scarring process presenting with fluid overload and low output, not acute pleuritic pain with fever and a rub.
Correct. Pericarditis weeks after myocardial infarction or post-cardiotomy (cardiac surgery) is Dressler syndrome, an inflammatory reaction to the injured tissue; aspirin plus colchicine treats it.
His wound looks clean, and a wound infection does not produce a friction rub with positional pericardial pain.
ruled out by a stated finding
Graft occlusion causes ischemic pressure pain and regional changes, not positional pain with a rub.

A.q: A 71-year-old woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy has fatigue and exercise intolerance along with leg edema, hepatomegaly and ascites, but her lungs are relatively clear. Which pattern of heart failure is expected to dominate in this condition?
opts: Left-sided failure brings pulmonary congestion, crackles and orthopnea to the fore. In restrictive cardiomyopathy right-sided failure often dominates instead.
Correct. Although filling pressures are raised in both ventricles, right heart failure is often more prominent and may dominate in restrictive cardiomyopathy, giving edema, hepatomegaly and ascites.
Systolic function is usually normal in restrictive cardiomyopathy; the problem is diastolic filling, and right-sided failure tends to dominate.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy reduces output because stiff ventricles fill poorly. The dominant pattern is right-sided failure, not a high-output state.

A.q: A 60-year-old woman with a prosthetic valve and a past episode of anaphylaxis to penicillin needs a dental cleaning and can take pills. Which prophylactic agent should be avoided?
opts: Azithromycin is an appropriate oral option for a penicillin-allergic patient, even after anaphylaxis to penicillin.
Correct. Cephalexin, cefazolin and ceftriaxone should not be used in patients with a history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria to penicillin or ampicillin.
Doxycycline is an appropriate oral option for a penicillin-allergic patient, even after anaphylaxis to penicillin.
Clarithromycin is an appropriate oral option for a penicillin-allergic patient, even after anaphylaxis to penicillin.

A.q: A 74-year-old woman with newly diagnosed deep vein thrombosis has chronic kidney disease with a creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min. Which approach should be avoided?
opts: Hospital admission for unfractionated heparin, given as a loading bolus then a continuous infusion, is the recommended approach for severe renal disease, so it is appropriate rather than one to avoid.
Unfractionated heparin is titrated to the activated partial thromboplastin time, so laboratory-guided adjustment is standard and appropriate rather than an error.
Heparin is given together with warfarin for at least five days and until the international normalized ratio is above 2 for at least 24 hours. This overlap is standard, not a mistake.

Correct. Patients with a creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min are hospitalized to start treatment, because renal insufficiency also excludes outpatient therapy. Starting at home is the approach to avoid.

A.q: A 59-year-old man in ventricular fibrillation arrest is shocked several times, and his rhythm changes to a flat line with no electrical activity in two leads. What does this change mean for his outlook?
opts: The change matters: asystole is a poor-prognosis rhythm, whereas fibrillation has the best prognosis of the arrest rhythms.
Correct. Ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation have the best prognosis of the arrest rhythms; asystole has a poor prognosis and is usually an end-of-life rhythm.
A flat line is not a successful conversion; there is no organized activity. It signals a much worse prognosis.
Asystole carries a poorer prognosis than ventricular fibrillation, not a better one.

A.q: What most commonly causes a lower extremity arteriovenous fistula?
opts: Trauma can cause an acquired fistula, but the most common lower extremity cause is iatrogenic injury from groin access during a procedure.
Correct. Lower extremity fistulas are most commonly iatrogenic, from using the groin (femoral vessels) for percutaneous arterial and venous access in endovascular procedures.
Fistulas created for dialysis are placed in the upper arm or forearm, generally preferred over the leg. Lower extremity fistulas usually follow groin access.
Congenital fistulas exist but are not the most common lower extremity cause. Most follow iatrogenic groin access for endovascular procedures.

A.q: A 40-year-old woman has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 182 with palpitations and mild anxiety. Her blood pressure is 128/80, oxygen saturation 98%, and she is alert without chest pain. Which treatment should be tried first?
opts: Amiodarone is tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, not as the first step in a stable narrow complex tachycardia.
Correct. Stable supraventricular tachycardia is treated first with a vagal maneuver, then adenosine (up to twice), keeping synchronized cardioversion for instability.
Adenosine comes second, after a vagal maneuver fails, in stable supraventricular tachycardia.
Synchronized cardioversion is reserved for the unstable patient; she is stable, so a vagal maneuver comes first.

B.q: A 52-year-old man becomes ill over 4 days with a temperature of 40.1 °C (104.2 °F), shaking chills and confusion. He looks toxic, a new loud regurgitant murmur is heard, and painless hemorrhagic macules appear on his soles, which are Janeway lesions (painless, nontender spots). Which form of infective endocarditis fits his course?
opts: Correct. Acute endocarditis is a hectically febrile illness from a virulent, invasive organism: rapid onset over 3-10 days, high fevers, systemic toxicity, rapid valve damage and seeding of extracardiac sites such as the skin.
Subacute disease is indolent: lower fevers, malaise and weight loss over weeks or months, slow structural damage and rare metastasis.
Libman-Sacks endocarditis is the non-infective lesion of systemic lupus erythematosus; it does not cause high fever, toxicity and septic emboli.
Device endocarditis means vegetation on a pacemaker or defibrillator, and no device is described; his 4-day toxic course is the acute form.

B.q: A 68-year-old man who started amlodipine for hypertension five weeks ago has bilateral, symmetric ankle swelling without warmth, redness or tenderness. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A D-dimer is a nonspecific test used when deep vein thrombosis is a real concern. With bilateral, noninflamed swelling after a new drug, the likelier explanation is the medication.
Review the medication as the cause

Correct. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine commonly cause edema, typically bilateral and without signs of inflammation. Recognizing drug-induced edema and reviewing the medication list is the appropriate step.
Symmetric swelling without warmth or tenderness after starting amlodipine is the classic picture of drug-induced edema, not of clot, which is usually unilateral. Imaging is not the first step.
Anticoagulation treats a confirmed clot and carries bleeding risk. Bilateral swelling with no inflammation after a new calcium channel blocker points to a drug effect, so a clot is unlikely.

B.q: Which patient with recurrent pericarditis is described as a candidate for anti-interleukin-1 therapy?
opts: Correct. Recurrent or colchicine-resistant disease, or steroid-dependent disease, with an inflammatory phenotype makes anakinra or rilonacept the preferred option.
Tamponade needs expedient pericardiocentesis, not a biologic. Anti-interleukin-1 therapy targets steroid-dependent or colchicine-resistant recurrence.
One with a normal C-reactive protein
A normal C-reactive protein argues against the inflammatory phenotype that anti-interleukin-1 therapy targets.
One with a first, mild episode
A first episode is treated with an anti-inflammatory plus colchicine for about 3 months. Anti-interleukin-1 therapy is for recurrent, resistant or steroid-dependent disease.

B.q: A 66-year-old woman with viridans streptococcal endocarditis had positive blood cultures on days 1 and 2 and her first negative culture on day 4. She asks how long her antibiotics will last. Which answer is most accurate?
opts: Correct. Therapy is typically 4-6 weeks counted from the first negative culture, here day 4, because all bacteria in the vegetation must be killed.
The clock does not start at admission; it starts at the first negative blood culture, which here was day 4.
Defervescence does not end therapy; the course is 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture.
Ten days is far too short to sterilize a vegetation; therapy runs 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture.

B.q: A 38-year-old woman has three months of worsening breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling. Dilated cardiomyopathy is suspected, but her 12-lead electrocardiogram is completely normal. Which interpretation of the normal tracing is most accurate?
opts: It points to restrictive disease instead
Restrictive cardiomyopathy commonly shows atrial fibrillation, bundle branch blocks or low voltage in amyloidosis, so a normal tracing does not point toward it.
It is what most dilated cardiomyopathy shows
The opposite holds: the electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in dilated cardiomyopathy, with arrhythmias or conduction delay such as left bundle branch block.
It excludes every cause of heart failure
A normal electrocardiogram cannot exclude heart failure in general. The test that excludes heart failure is a B-type natriuretic peptide below 100 pg/mL.
It makes dilated cardiomyopathy very unlikely

Correct. The electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in dilated cardiomyopathy, showing atrial fibrillation, premature ventricular contractions or left bundle branch block, so a normal tracing almost rules the diagnosis out.

B.q: A 50-year-old woman with a diagnosed leg deep vein thrombosis, not yet treated, develops sudden shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. Which complication has occurred?
opts: Correct. Part of the thrombus can break off and travel to the lungs, causing a pulmonary embolism, the most important complication of deep vein thrombosis. Sudden breathlessness and pleuritic pain in this setting should prompt that concern.
Post-thrombotic syndrome is symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency that appears 6 to 24 months after a clot. It develops slowly in the leg and does not cause sudden breathlessness.
Infarction of the heart is arterial, and nothing in this scenario suggests it. A known leg clot with sudden dyspnea and pleuritic pain points to embolization to the pulmonary arteries.

Septic thrombophlebitis is an infected superficial vein, marked by high fever, purulent drainage and redness spreading beyond the vein, usually after cannulation. It does not produce acute breathlessness.

B.q: A 75-year-old man is newly diagnosed with restrictive cardiomyopathy caused by hemochromatosis, with iron deposited in the heart tissue. He has congestion and fatigue. Which is the first principle of his management?
opts: Correct. Management of restrictive cardiomyopathy begins with treating the underlying disorder, such as iron storage in hemochromatosis, with cautious diuretics, rate-slowing drugs and anticoagulation added as needed.
Systolic function is usually normal in restrictive cardiomyopathy, and an inotrope does not address the stiff filling. The first principle is treating the cause.
Myectomy relieves septal outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Restrictive disease is managed first by treating its underlying cause.
Exercise does not treat infiltrative or storage disease of the heart. Restrictive cardiomyopathy management starts with the underlying disorder.

B.q: A 67-year-old man has repeated dizziness and near-fainting while climbing stairs. His electrocardiogram shows the PR interval lengthening until a beat is dropped, in a repeating pattern. He takes no atrioventricular nodal blocking drugs, and no reversible cause is found. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Correct. Mobitz type I needs no treatment unless symptoms are debilitating; for symptomatic patients with no reversible cause, a permanent pacemaker is considered.
Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic for ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation. Symptomatic Mobitz type I is managed with a pacemaker.
Cardioversion terminates tachycardias. A symptomatic conduction block is paced rather than shocked.
Reassurance fits silent Mobitz type I. Recurrent near-fainting with exertion makes him a candidate for a permanent pacemaker.

B.q: A 69-year-old man has sudden severe pain in his right leg. Pulses are absent below the knee. Which examination finding is often the earliest neurologic sign of acute vascular insufficiency?
opts: Sensory loss over the foot's dorsum
Correct. Light-touch sensory fibers are highly susceptible to ischemia, so sensory deficits over the dorsum of the foot are often the earliest neurologic sign of acute vascular insufficiency.
Loss of hair on the shin
Hair loss is a chronic peripheral artery disease finding from long-standing poor flow. In acute ischemia the earliest neurologic sign is dorsal foot sensory loss.
Profound paralysis marks an irreversibly ischemic limb, a late finding. Sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot appears earlier because light-touch fibers are most sensitive.
Reflex testing is not named as the early sign. Light-touch sensory fibers fail first, so loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot comes earliest.

Heparin is reversed by protamine sulfate, not idarucizumab. Idarucizumab reverses the direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran.

B.q: A 61-year-old woman with recurrent pericarditis over several years now has leg edema, ascites and an elevated jugular venous pressure. Constrictive pericarditis is suspected. Which echocardiogram finding would best support it?
opts: A dilated, poorly contracting ventricle is dilated cardiomyopathy; constriction keeps systolic function and restricts filling.
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Constriction shows a septal bounce and a thick pericardium.
Right ventricular diastolic collapse is the echocardiographic sign of tamponade, from fluid under pressure, not constriction.
Septal bounce toward the left ventricle

Correct. Echocardiographic features of constriction are increased pericardial thickness, abnormal septal motion or bounce toward the left ventricle, pronounced respiratory variation in ventricular filling and moderate biatrial enlargement.

B.q: After a positive D-dimer in the low likelihood Wells category, which test comes next?
opts: Venography is invasive and has been replaced by ultrasound. A positive D-dimer is followed by venous duplex ultrasound.
Repeating a nonspecific test adds nothing. A positive D-dimer is followed by venous duplex ultrasound.
The work-up stops only after a negative D-dimer. A positive result means fibrinolysis is occurring somewhere, so ultrasound follows.
Correct. A positive D-dimer is nonspecific, so it is followed by ultrasound of the leg; a positive ultrasound gives the diagnosis and a negative one rules it out.

B.q: A 44-year-old man arrives with a temperature of 40.2 °C (104.4 °F), rigors and a new murmur, and he looks toxic. Acute endocarditis is suspected. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Two cultures within 1-2 hours, then antibiotics
Correct. If the presentation suggests acute endocarditis, two cultures are drawn within the first 1-2 hours, and empiric antibiotics are started only after the cultures are drawn.
Untreated acute endocarditis can be fatal within weeks and destroys valves rapidly; observation is not appropriate.
Echocardiography matters, but the first step in a toxic patient is cultures within 1-2 hours, then empiric antibiotics.
Antibiotics given before cultures can leave them negative and lose the organism; cultures come first.

B.q: A 6-year-old with repaired congenital heart disease has 3 weeks of low-grade fever, fatigue, joint aches and weight loss. A new murmur is heard. Which organism most commonly causes endocarditis in this age group?
opts: Enterococci are less common in children than in adults; viridans streptococci lead after age 1 with congenital heart disease.
Candida is tied to neonatal central lines and hyperalimentation, not indolent disease in older children.
Correct. Children over 1 year with congenital heart disease develop indolent viridans group streptococcal disease; Staphylococcus aureus comes next.
Group B streptococci are a less common neonatal organism, not the leading organism after age 1.

B.q: Which organism is a classic cause of acute infective endocarditis?
opts: Correct. Acute infective endocarditis is caused by virulent organisms: beta-hemolytic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible or methicillin-resistant), sometimes Staphylococcus lugdunensis, and enterococci.
Viridans streptococci are the classic cause of subacute endocarditis, with an indolent course after dental sources of bacteremia.
Streptococcus gallolyticus is the gastrointestinal-source organism. The classic acute organism is Staphylococcus aureus.
The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group causes subacute endocarditis, not the rapidly destructive acute form.

B.q: An 81-year-old man has known tachy-brady syndrome (a fast rhythm alternating with slow rates and pauses) and asks which fast rhythm is behind his palpitations. An ambulatory monitor is arranged. Which rhythm is it most likely to record during the fast episodes?
opts: A junctional rhythm is slow and regular, usually 40 to 60, not the fast phase of tachy-brady syndrome.
Ventricular tachycardia can occur in some patients, who then need a defibrillator with the pacemaker, but atrial fibrillation is the most common.
Flutter is an organized atrial circuit with sawtooth waves; it is not the usual fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome.
Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome the tachyarrhythmia that alternates with bradycardia or pauses is most commonly atrial fibrillation.

B.q: A 58-year-old man with acute pericarditis is starting ibuprofen and colchicine. He has a history of dyspepsia. Which addition to his regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Antibiotics have no role in idiopathic or viral pericarditis. Gastrointestinal protection is the needed addition.
Correct. Gastrointestinal protection is provided with anti-inflammatory therapy, for example a proton pump inhibitor, because these drugs reduce the stomach's protective prostaglandins.
Anticoagulation is not part of pericarditis therapy, and patients already on anticoagulants are a higher-risk group.
Diuretics treat fluid overload in constrictive disease, not acute pericarditis. He needs gastrointestinal protection.

B.q: A 69-year-old man receiving an unfractionated heparin infusion for deep vein thrombosis develops life-threatening bleeding. Which agent reverses the heparin?
opts: Andexanet alfa reverses the direct factor Xa inhibitors apixaban and rivaroxaban. Heparin is reversed instead by protamine sulfate.

Correct. Protamine sulfate is the reversal agent for unfractionated and low molecular weight heparin in life-threatening or intracranial hemorrhage; dabigatran, the factor Xa inhibitors and warfarin have other reversal options.
Oral vitamin K is one of the warfarin reversal options. Heparin has its own reversal agent, protamine sulfate, used for life-threatening bleeding.
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, and does nothing for heparin. The agent that neutralizes heparin is protamine sulfate.

B.q: A 70-year-old man has an asymptomatic infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 3.4 cm on ultrasound. Which follow-up is most appropriate?
opts: Ultrasound or computed tomography every six to 12 months is for aneurysms of 4.0 to 5.4 cm. At 3.4 cm the interval is every three years.
Correct. Once identified, an aneurysm is followed for size and growth; a 3.0 to 3.9 cm aneurysm is imaged with ultrasound every three years.
Elective repair is for 5.0 cm or larger in women and over 5.5 cm in men, or rapid growth. A 3.4 cm aneurysm needs surveillance, every three years.
Every identified aneurysm needs routine follow-up of size and growth rate. At 3.4 cm that means ultrasound every three years.

B.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
B.q: A 73-year-old man who lives at home has 3 weeks of low-grade fever and a new murmur. He has had no recent hospital stay, procedure or urinary symptoms, and no primary source of infection is found. Two separate blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis. How do these cultures count under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: A positive culture that misses the major criterion is minor microbiologic evidence, but community-acquired enterococci without a primary focus in two cultures meet the major one.
Correct. Community-acquired enterococci in the absence of a primary focus count as a typical organism, so growth from two separate blood cultures meets the major blood culture criterion.
Single cultures of coagulase-negative staphylococci or diphtheroids are excluded as contaminants; enterococci in two separate cultures are a typical organism.
Blood cultures count on their own; echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement is the other, separate major criterion, not a condition for this one.

B.q: A 52-year-old man who smokes and has diabetes and hypertension asks whether he is too young to have peripheral artery disease. Which age threshold applies to him?
opts: Seventy is later than either threshold. People with risk factors such as smoking and diabetes are at risk from age 50, and those without from over 60.
Over 60 is the threshold for people without other risk factors. With smoking, diabetes and hypertension, the threshold drops to age 50.
Correct. Peripheral artery disease is a concern from age 50 in people with risk factors such as smoking, diabetes and hypertension, and from over 60 in people without other risk factors.
A family history is a risk factor, but 40 is not the stated threshold. The age cut-offs are 50 with risk factors and over 60 without them.

B.q: A 64-year-old woman has two weeks of exertional breathlessness and chest pressure. Her electrocardiogram shows a left bundle branch block; a tracing from last year was normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. A new left bundle branch block should always be considered a sign of pathology, so it is worked up for the underlying cardiac disease or injury rather than dismissed.
Cardioversion terminates tachycardias; a conduction block with a normal rate is not shocked. The new block needs a workup.
Some new right bundle branch blocks occur without heart disease, but a new left bundle branch block is a sign of pathology that needs evaluation.
Left bundle branch block is usually not paced unless it is symptomatic with reduced ejection fraction, which calls for a biventricular device after evaluation.

B.q: A 70-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has three months of progressive hoarseness. A chest radiograph shows widening of the mediastinal shadow. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: An abdominal aneurysm causes abdominal, back or flank pain and cannot involve the recurrent laryngeal nerve or widen the mediastinum.
A descending aneurysm compresses the trachea or esophagus, giving dyspnea, stridor, cough or dysphagia. Hoarseness points to the arch.
Correct. Thoracic aneurysm symptoms depend on location: an arch aneurysm causes hoarseness by involving the recurrent laryngeal nerve, and the chest film shows a widened mediastinum.
An ascending aneurysm causes aortic regurgitation and heart failure rather than hoarseness. Hoarseness localizes the aneurysm to the arch.

B.q: A 27-year-old woman has had 20 minutes of sudden palpitations. Her heart rate is 188, blood pressure 122/76, and she is alert with no chest pain or breathlessness. The electrocardiogram shows a regular narrow complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. Which is the most appropriate first step?
opts: Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for the hemodynamically unstable patient; she is alert with a normal blood pressure.
Procainamide is reserved for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; a stable narrow complex tachycardia starts with a vagal maneuver.
Correct. A stable, regular narrow complex tachycardia above 160 with hidden P waves is supraventricular tachycardia, and the first-line treatment when stable is a vagal maneuver, then adenosine.
Adenosine is the second step for stable supraventricular tachycardia, given if a vagal maneuver fails.

B.q: A 76-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes has nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and a high CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke risk) score. Which anticoagulant class is preferred?
opts: Warfarin is an alternative with a target ratio of 2 to 3, but direct oral anticoagulants are preferred in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation.
Aspirin is an antiplatelet drug, not one of the anticoagulants listed for atrial fibrillation.
Older age raises stroke risk rather than ruling out anticoagulation; a high score means she typically needs it.
Correct. Direct oral anticoagulants (dabigatran, apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban) are preferred in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation; a high stroke-risk score means she needs anticoagulation.

B.q: An 81-year-old man with 3 months of weight loss presents with dyspnea and a large pericardial effusion. He has had no recent viral illness, chest surgery or radiation. Which etiology should be most strongly suspected?
opts: Rheumatic pancarditis follows streptococcal infection in younger patients and is not the concern here; malignancy is.
Correct. In older adults there is a higher index of suspicion for malignancy, especially with an effusion or tamponade, and his weight loss without a viral prodrome reinforces it.
Coxsackievirus is a classic cause of viral pericarditis and would usually follow a viral illness, which he has not had. Malignancy fits this older man.
ruled out by a stated finding
Dressler syndrome follows myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery, which he has not had.

B.q: A 61-year-old woman with long-standing pulmonary hypertension from scleroderma has a right bundle branch block on her electrocardiogram. Which of her conditions is a named cause of this block?
opts: Raynaud phenomenon affects digital vessels, not cardiac conduction. Pulmonary hypertension is the named cause.
Osteoporosis has no link to cardiac conduction. Pulmonary hypertension is the named cause of right bundle branch block.
Reflux disease is not a cause of bundle branch block. Pulmonary hypertension is.
Correct. Pulmonary hypertension is a named cause of right bundle branch block, by chronically straining the right ventricle and its conduction system.

B.q: A 32-year-old man has typical acute viral pericarditis with stable vital signs and no high-risk features. A transthoracic echocardiogram is ordered. Which result is most expected?
opts: A normal study or only a small effusion
Correct. The echocardiogram is often normal in acute pericarditis unless there is an associated effusion, and the chest radiograph is typically normal; the diagnosis is primarily clinical.
Apical ballooning with a normal base
Apical ballooning is stress cardiomyopathy. Acute pericarditis usually has a normal echocardiogram.
A thick pericardium with septal bounce
Septal bounce with pericardial thickening suggests constrictive pericarditis, a late complication, not acute disease.
Right ventricular diastolic collapse indicates tamponade, which this stable patient does not have.

B.q: A 24-year-old woman with chest pain and breathlessness after a recent viral illness is being evaluated for myocarditis. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia. Which laboratory result would indicate cardiac myonecrosis?
opts: A B-type natriuretic peptide below 100 pg/mL argues against heart failure; it is not a marker of myonecrosis. Elevated troponin is.
The blood count in myocarditis shows leukocytosis, a raised rather than low white cell count, and it does not measure myocardial injury. Troponin does.

Correct. Serum troponin is the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis in myocarditis. The rest of the work-up adds leukocytosis on the blood count, a possibly elevated sedimentation rate and electrocardiogram changes.
The erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated in myocarditis, and in either case it does not indicate myonecrosis. Troponin is the marker of heart muscle injury.

B.q: A 20-year-old man has just been diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy on echocardiography. He has two younger sisters and a brother. His mother had unexplained sudden death at 44. Which step for his family is most appropriate?
opts: Most hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, so his siblings each carry a real risk and should be evaluated.
Autosomal dominant inheritance affects both sexes, and males are affected more often than females. Every first-degree relative should be evaluated.
Many patients are asymptomatic and are found only through family evaluation, and sudden death can be the first event. Relatives are evaluated whether or not they have symptoms.

Correct. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, so one affected parent is enough to pass it on, and detection in a family member is a common reason evaluation of relatives begins.

B.q: A 70-year-old woman has Mobitz type II block found on a routine tracing; she has no symptoms. Her family prefers to avoid procedures. Which approach should be avoided?
opts: Referral is appropriate for a pacemaker evaluation. The approach to avoid is simple observation of Mobitz type II.
A permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for Mobitz type II, so it should not be avoided; observation alone should be.

Correct. Observation alone should be avoided because Mobitz type II is considered dangerous even without symptoms; its progression is unpredictable, so the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.
Checking for drugs that slow conduction is reasonable and not harmful. What should be avoided is observation without a pacemaker.

B.q: Adenosine slows a tachycardia and reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Which drug is used?
opts: More adenosine blocks only the normal atrioventricular node and leaves the accessory pathway to carry the fibrillation; procainamide is used.
Magnesium is for torsades de pointes; pre-excited atrial fibrillation is treated with procainamide.

Correct. When slowing from adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, intravenous procainamide is used and adenosine is not repeated; adenosine and the other nodal blockers leave the accessory pathway unopposed.
Atropine speeds the heart and treats unstable bradycardia; it would worsen a pre-excited tachycardia, which needs procainamide.

B.q: A 68-year-old man is 4 days into his recovery from a large anterior myocardial infarction when he suddenly becomes hypotensive, with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. Which is the most likely explanation?
opts: Constriction develops over months and does not cause sudden collapse days after an infarction.

Dressler syndrome is an inflammatory pericarditis weeks after infarction, with pain and a rub, not sudden collapse with the Beck triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds) on day 4.
Massive pulmonary embolism can mimic acute tamponade, but muffled heart sounds days after a large anterior infarction point to free-wall rupture filling the pericardium.
Correct. Free-wall rupture after myocardial infarction is a recognized cause of tamponade, alongside acute pericarditis, iatrogenic injury, trauma, malignancy and aortic dissection.

B.q: Which electrical treatment is delivered for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion times the shock to a consistent QRS and suits unstable monomorphic rhythm with a pulse. Polymorphic rhythm is defibrillated.
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable and its QRS shape keeps changing, so it is defibrillated (unsynchronized) even when a pulse is present.
Transcutaneous pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms such as Mobitz type II and complete block. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is treated with unsynchronized defibrillation.
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, so there is no trial of drugs first: it is defibrillated, and an antiarrhythmic or beta blocker may be added afterward.

B.q: A 71-year-old woman hospitalized after surgery has had a peripheral intravenous catheter in her arm for a week. She has a high fever, fluctuance over a tender vein, and redness spreading well past the vein. Which is the most appropriate approach?
opts: Treat as infection within the vein

Correct. High fever, fluctuance or purulence, and erythema extending far beyond the vein after cannulation indicate septic thrombophlebitis, which needs antimicrobial treatment and removal of the catheter rather than simple phlebitis care.
Compresses and ibuprofen with a recheck in 7 to 10 days
That plan is for uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis. Fever, fluctuance and spreading redness indicate infection within the vein, which needs antimicrobial therapy and removal of the catheter.

Anticoagulation addresses extensive clot burden in sterile thrombophlebitis. High fever with fluctuance and spreading redness indicates infection, whose core treatment is antimicrobial therapy with removal of the catheter.
Reassure that the process is self-limited
Sterile superficial thrombophlebitis is usually mild, but this presentation signals infection within the vein. That is uncommon without cannulation and requires treatment for infection.

B.q: A 79-year-old man has enterococcal endocarditis of the aortic valve after recurrent urinary infections. Which outcome is he at notable risk for?
opts: Lung emboli are not the outcome singled out for enterococci; antibiotic resistance makes them hard to treat, with valve replacement in about 30-40%.
Correct. Enterococcal endocarditis is difficult to treat because of antibiotic resistance, and major complications with need for valve replacement occur in about 30-40%.
Enterococcal endocarditis does not cure itself; it is difficult to treat because of resistance.
Enterococci are not the low-risk organism; antibiotic resistance makes them hard to treat, with valve replacement in 30-40%.

B.q: A 32-year-old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant sits in a car for nine hours and develops left calf swelling and pain. Her pregnancy supplies a hypercoagulable state and the long ride supplies venous stasis. Which additional component would complete the Virchow triad?
opts: Venous stasis is already present from nine hours of sitting still, so it cannot be the additional component. The one still missing is endothelial trauma, injury to the vessel wall.
Arterial thrombosis is a clot in an artery and is not a component of the Virchow triad. The venous component still absent in this scenario is endothelial trauma.

Correct. The Virchow triad is venous stasis, hypercoagulable state and endothelial trauma. Pregnancy and the car ride supply two components, so the missing one is injury to the vein wall, as from trauma, surgery, burns or injection.
Pregnancy already supplies the hypercoagulable state by raising clotting tendency, so it is present rather than missing. The component still absent is endothelial trauma.

B.q: A 50-year-old woman with symptomatic varicose veins has worn stockings and exercised faithfully for several months with persistent aching. Duplex ultrasound confirms great saphenous vein reflux. Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
opts: Observation alone leaves her persistent aching untreated after a full trial of stockings and exercise. Once that conservative trial has failed, venous ablation therapy is offered.

Correct. A trial of conservative therapy with stockings is generally done for weeks to months before venous ablation is offered. She has finished that trial with persistent aching, and duplex confirms reflux; the goal is better symptoms and appearance.
Flavonoids are used to increase venous tone, but no oral medication has yet been proven useful for venous disease. With reflux confirmed after failed stockings, ablation is offered.
Valvuloplasty is a chronic venous insufficiency operation that is only occasionally successful and carries a high incidence of postoperative deep vein thrombosis. Her reflux is treated by ablation.
