B.q: A 62-year-old man started a new blood pressure medication two weeks ago. He now feels tired, and his pulse is 46 and regular, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Thyroid tests are normal. Which medication is the most likely cause?
opts: A thiazide diuretic does not slow the sinus node; the listed bradycardic drugs are beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin.
Lisinopril, an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, is not among the drug causes of sinus bradycardia; beta blockers are.
Correct. Beta blockers such as metoprolol, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin are the drug causes of sinus bradycardia; a new one two weeks ago is the likely culprit.
Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker; the calcium channel blockers that cause bradycardia are the nondihydropyridines, verapamil and diltiazem.

B.q: A 16-year-old girl with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has had an episode of fainting during basketball practice and brief runs of ventricular tachycardia on monitoring. She wants to keep playing on her competitive school team. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Hydration is advised in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, but it does not make competitive play safe for a high-risk adolescent. Activity restriction is the strategy.
Activity restriction given her high risk

Correct. Activity restriction for high-risk individuals is an adolescent strategy; her exertional syncope marks high risk of sudden death, which in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is highest in preadolescents and adolescents and related to extreme exertion.
The outflow murmur changes with blood flow in the heart, so a softer murmur does not mean lower risk. Her syncope on exertion identifies high risk of sudden death and calls for activity restriction.
Competitive play on a beta blocker
A beta blocker treats outflow obstruction but does not license competitive sport in a high-risk patient. Sudden death relates to extreme exertion, so activity is restricted.

B.q: What does the transthoracic echocardiogram show in Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: Enlarged atria with near-normal, stiff ventricles fit restrictive cardiomyopathy, not stress cardiomyopathy.
Septal wall of 1.5 cm or more
Wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more confirms hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, not stress cardiomyopathy.
Four-chamber dilation with thin walls is dilated cardiomyopathy. Stress cardiomyopathy gives regional mid and apical hypokinesis.
Correct. The transthoracic echocardiogram shows wall-motion abnormality, hypokinesis or akinesis of the midsegment and apical segment of the left ventricle.

B.q: A 34-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle crash with a large thigh wound and heavy blood loss. He has no pulse. The monitor shows a regular narrow-complex rhythm at 110 per minute. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Asystole is a flat line. This monitor shows an organized rhythm, so it is pulseless electrical activity.
Sinus tachycardia has a pulse. Without a pulse, the same organized rhythm is pulseless electrical activity.
ruled out by a stated finding
Fibrillation is chaotic with no organized complexes. A regular narrow rhythm without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity.
Correct. An organized rhythm on which a pulse would be expected, but with no pulse, is pulseless electrical activity; hypovolemia is one of its two leading causes in adults.

B.q: Which aortic condition can also shed emboli that cause blue toe syndrome?
opts: A femoral pseudoaneurysm presents with pain from swelling or nerve compression. Abdominal aortic aneurysm is the listed embolic source.
Regurgitation is a valve leak, not an embolic source here. Abdominal aortic aneurysm can cause embolic blue toe.
Carotid emboli go to the brain and eye. Abdominal aortic aneurysm can shed emboli to the toes.
Correct. A symptomatic, unruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm can produce embolic phenomena leading to blue toe syndrome, besides pain, early satiety and groin pain.

B.q: A 70-year-old smoker has a painful, dry, punched-out ulcer at the tip of his second toe with minimal bleeding and surrounding black necrotic tissue. It started as a minor scrape months ago. Which complication is he at risk of?
opts: Correct. Ischemic skin ulcers fail to heal because blood supply cannot meet the demands of healing tissue; they sit at the most distal sites, are often ringed by dry gangrene, and can lead to osteomyelitis.
Aortic dissection is an intimal tear with a false lumen, presenting with tearing chest pain. The complication of a nonhealing ischemic toe ulcer is osteomyelitis.
Venous insufficiency is a separate cause of leg swelling, not a complication of an arterial ulcer. A nonhealing ischemic toe ulcer can progress to osteomyelitis.
A pseudoaneurysm follows arterial laceration, typically by a catheterization needle. A chronic ischemic toe ulcer threatens bone, leading to osteomyelitis.

B.q: A 16-year-old boy collapses briefly during a basketball game and recovers within a minute. Blood pressure and heart rate are normal. There is a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the left sternal border in the fourth intercostal space that does not radiate to the carotids; it grows louder when he stands and softer when he squats. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Restrictive cardiomyopathy is rare, presents late with right-sided congestion and big atria, and does not produce an outflow murmur that changes with standing and squatting.
Myocarditis follows a flulike illness with acute heart failure and elevated troponin. A posture-sensitive outflow murmur in an athlete points to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Correct. Exertional syncope in an adolescent with an outflow murmur at the left sternal border that does not reach the carotids, louder with standing and softer with squatting, is obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Dilated cardiomyopathy gives heart failure symptoms with a displaced apical impulse, a third heart sound and regurgitant murmurs, not a dynamic outflow murmur that changes with posture.

B.q: A 62-year-old woman who had a left leg deep vein thrombosis after a hip fracture ten years ago reports a heavy, aching left lower leg by evening that eases when she elevates it. Examination shows pitting edema, shiny taut skin at the ankle and brownish pigmentation. Pedal pulses are strong. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Progressive pitting edema with dull discomfort worse on standing, shiny taut ankle skin and brownish pigmentation after a prior deep vein thrombosis are the classic picture of chronic venous insufficiency.
Arterial disease causes exertional cramping relieved by rest and weak pulses, and pitting edema is not its feature. Strong pulses with edema and pigmentation point to venous disease.
Lymphedema is unilateral, lacks varicosities, and brawny hemosiderin staining is rare in it. Pitting edema with brown pigmentation after a prior clot is venous insufficiency.
An acute clot causes new swelling with pain and warmth over days. Ten years of slowly progressive edema with skin changes reflects chronic venous hypertension instead.

B.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
B.q: When is the dental prophylaxis dose given?
opts: A dose after the procedure misses the bacteremia it is meant to prevent; it is given 30-60 minutes before.
A dose a week early would be gone by the procedure. It is given 30-60 minutes beforehand.
Correct. The single prophylactic dose is given 30-60 minutes before the procedure, so the drug is circulating when the transient bacteremia occurs.
Prophylaxis is a single dose, not a month of daily antibiotics; it is given 30-60 minutes before the procedure.

B.q: A 64-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has sudden, severe, tearing chest pain radiating to his back. Blood pressure is 184/106. Imaging confirms an aortic dissection. Which blood pressure goal applies?
opts: Keeping systolic pressure above 140 mmHg does not stop progression of the dissection. Management lowers systolic pressure to 100 to 120 mmHg.
Correct. Management stops progression by reducing blood pressure, bringing systolic pressure to 100 to 120 mmHg with a beta blocker such as esmolol or a vasodilator such as nitroprusside.
A systolic pressure below 80 mmHg is far under the target range. Management reduces systolic pressure to 100 to 120 mmHg to stop progression of the dissection.

B.q: A 54-year-old man has stable dilated cardiomyopathy of two years' duration with no systemic illness and no recent change in his heart function. He has read about heart biopsies online and asks whether he should have one. What is the role of a heart muscle biopsy for him?
opts: Correct. Biopsy is not used routinely in dilated cardiomyopathy and is rarely useful. Its indications are a recent onset of rapidly deteriorating function or a systemic disease that can involve the heart.
The gold standard for his disease
Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard for myocarditis, not for stable dilated cardiomyopathy, where it is rarely useful and not done routinely.
Echocardiography comes first and shows the dilated, thin-walled ventricle. Biopsy, if ever used, is reserved for rapid deterioration or suspected systemic disease.
Dilated cardiomyopathy is diagnosed with echocardiography, electrocardiogram, radiograph and laboratory tests; biopsy is not required and is kept for rapid deterioration or systemic disease.

opts: Enterococci cause about 4% of device endocarditis, far behind coagulase-negative staphylococci.

The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms come from the upper respiratory tract and are not a leading device organism; coagulase-negative staphylococci lead at about 41%.
Streptococci cause only about 2% of device endocarditis; skin staphylococci dominate.

Correct. Device endocarditis is caused mostly by coagulase-negative staphylococci (about 41%) and Staphylococcus aureus (about 36%), and it can appear within weeks of implantation or a generator change.

Correct. Recurrent pericarditis affects about 15 to 30% of patients after acute pericarditis, which is why completing the full course and recognizing symptoms early matter.
Sixty percent overstates the risk. About 15 to 30% of patients have a recurrence.
Recurrence is common but far from universal: it follows about 15 to 30% of acute episodes, so most patients never have a second episode.

B.q: Which causes should be checked first in a patient with frequent premature ventricular contractions?
opts: Dehydration and fever are not the named causes. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalances head the list for premature ventricular contractions.

Correct. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalances (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia) are the main causes, so new frequent premature ventricular contractions call for checking oxygen and electrolytes.

Hypertension and diabetes drive degenerative conduction disease. Premature ventricular contractions come mainly from hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance.

Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. A magnesium infusion follows the first push.

opts: Physical therapy may help mobility, but the recommended consult for a symptomatic malignant effusion is palliative care.
Endocrinology addresses thyroid causes such as myxedema. Palliative care is recommended here.

Correct. Symptomatic malignant pericardial effusion carries a limited life expectancy (median 2 to 4 months) and often recurs; a palliative care consult is recommended to improve outcomes and quality of life.
Rheumatology helps autoimmune effusions. A malignant effusion calls for palliative care.

opts: A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; flutter at 140 needs rate control with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
A beta or calcium channel blocker
Correct. Hemodynamically stable atrial flutter is rate-controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker; rate control is the first goal, though harder to achieve than in fibrillation.
Adenosine is used for reentrant supraventricular tachycardia; stable flutter is rate-controlled.
Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable flutter; she is stable, so rate control comes first.

opts: A junctional rhythm is a steady slow rhythm at 40 to 60 with inverted or hidden P waves, not alternating early beats.
Premature ventricular beats are early, wide and bizarre with no P wave; hers have abnormal P waves and narrow QRS complexes.
ruled out by a stated finding
Flutter shows continuous sawtooth waves at 250 or more, not alternating normal and early beats.
Correct. Early beats with an abnormal P wave and narrow QRS are premature atrial contractions (common in chronic lung disease), and an ectopic beat every other beat is bigeminy.

opts: Exertion can trigger episodes, but blanket exercise avoidance is not the advice; limiting caffeine, alcohol and stimulants is.
Correct. Nodal reentry may occur spontaneously or with exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists and sympathomimetics, so limiting her known triggers is sensible counseling.
A pacemaker is for slow rhythms; nodal reentry is a tachycardia managed with trigger avoidance and vagal maneuvers.
Nodal reentry does not raise stroke risk the way atrial fibrillation does; no anticoagulant is needed.

opts: Metformin is not among the medication causes of pericardial effusion, which include doxorubicin, minoxidil and phenytoin.

Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism, and myxedema is itself a cause of effusion; the drug is not a cause. Doxorubicin is a listed medication cause.
Correct. Medication causes of pericardial effusion include doxorubicin, minoxidil, phenytoin, and hydralazine and procainamide through drug-induced lupus.

opts: A deficit lasting beyond 24 hours no longer fits the transient attack. It must resolve within 24 hours.
A week-long global state is not the definition. The attack is a focal deficit resolving within 24 hours.
Headache alone without focal loss is not the definition. It is a focal deficit lasting under 24 hours.

opts: Antiarrhythmics are kept for symptomatic episodes after other options. Silent runs call for optimizing his heart failure.
Cardioversion is for sustained, unstable tachycardia. Brief silent runs are managed by optimizing underlying disease.
Correct. Asymptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia is managed by optimizing treatment of the underlying cardiac comorbidities; it is not by itself an indication for a defibrillator.
Non-sustained ventricular tachycardia in and of itself is not an indication for a defibrillator. His underlying disease should be optimized.

C.q: Which description fits recurrent pericarditis?
opts: Symptoms persist without remission for up to 3 months
Persistence without a sustained remission from 4 to 6 weeks up to 3 months is incessant pericarditis; recurrence needs a symptom-free gap first.
Symptoms return after a symptom-free gap of 4 to 6 weeks
Correct. Recurrent pericarditis is when symptoms of acute pericarditis return after a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer, which separates it from incessant disease.
Symptoms persist without any remission past 3 months
Unbroken symptoms beyond 3 months define chronic pericarditis. Recurrence requires a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer before the symptoms return.
Constriction persists after an effusion has been drained
Persistent constriction after drainage of an effusion is effusive-constrictive pericarditis. Recurrent pericarditis is a return of symptoms after a 4-to-6-week symptom-free gap.

C.q: A 29-year-old woman who injects drugs has 5 days of high fever and rigors. Transthoracic imaging shows a large vegetation on the tricuspid valve, and three sets of blood cultures are drawn from separate sites. Which organism are the cultures most likely to grow?
opts: Candida is a fungal cause linked to immunocompromise and central lines; the dominant organism in injection drug use is Staphylococcus aureus.
Viridans streptococci follow oral sources such as dental work. Injection through the skin introduces Staphylococcus aureus.
Correct. In people who inject drugs, Staphylococcus aureus causes more than 60% of all endocarditis and 80-90% of cases where the tricuspid valve is infected.
Enterococci come from the genitourinary tract. Tricuspid endocarditis in a person who injects drugs is Staphylococcus aureus in 80-90%.

opts: His coronary arteries are normal, so plaque rupture is not the cause. The angina comes from outflow obstruction and the oxygen demand of thick muscle.
Outflow obstruction and thick muscle demand

Correct. Angina without coronary disease in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy comes from left ventricular outflow tract obstruction and the increased oxygen consumption of hypertrophied muscle, causing ischemia during exertion.
A dilated, thin-walled ventricle is dilated cardiomyopathy. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy the ventricle is thick, and its oxygen demand plus outflow obstruction cause angina.
Pericardial inflammation is a differential for restrictive disease, not the source of exertional angina here. Outflow obstruction and hypertrophy drive it.

C.q: A 69-year-old woman is brought in by her daughter for 2 days of new confusion. She has a fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), a new murmur and conjunctival petechiae (pinpoint hemorrhages on the conjunctiva). Brain imaging shows multiple small scattered lesions without a large stroke. Which mechanism best explains her confusion?
opts: No sedating drug is described; fever, a murmur, petechiae and scattered brain lesions point to septic emboli from a vegetation.
Correct. Vegetations shower septic emboli into the systemic circulation; the brain is affected (ischemic stroke, abscess, hemorrhage, meningitis), producing neurologic deficits such as confusion.
Meningitis is one cerebral complication, but scattered small lesions with a new murmur and petechiae point to septic emboli from a vegetation.
No conduction block is described; scattered lesions with fever and a murmur point to septic emboli.

Mycoplasma is a bacterial cause of pericarditis. The fungal causes include Histoplasma, Aspergillus, Blastomyces, Coccidioides and Candida.
Echinococcus is a parasitic cause, listed with amebic disease and Toxoplasma. Histoplasma is the fungal cause here.
Correct. The fungal causes listed are Histoplasma, Aspergillus, Blastomyces, Coccidioides and Candida; they are uncommon compared with idiopathic or viral disease.

opts: Correct. Stopping progression of the dissection means reducing blood pressure, with systolic pressure brought to 100 to 120 mmHg using a beta blocker such as esmolol or a vasodilator such as nitroprusside.
Intravenous heparin is the medical therapy for acute limb ischemia. A dissection needs its systolic pressure reduced to 100 to 120 mmHg, for example with intravenous esmolol.
Cilostazol is an oral drug that suppresses platelet aggregation in peripheral artery disease. An acute dissection is treated by lowering blood pressure, for example with intravenous esmolol.

C.q: A 66-year-old man has a continuous bruit and a palpable thrill (a vibration felt over the skin) over the left femoral region, with mild leg swelling. He has not had dialysis and has no trauma history. His only recent procedure was an endovascular repair of an iliac artery performed through the left groin. Which is the most likely cause?

Created fistulas are made for hemodialysis and are usually in the upper arm or forearm. This man has no dialysis history and the fistula sits at the femoral puncture.

Better exercise tolerance and quality of life

Rehabilitation supports medication adherence rather than replacing drugs. It aims at exercise tolerance and quality of life.

opts: Asthma causes wheeze and dyspnea, not ascites with a raised jugular venous pressure.

Pneumonia is a differential of acute pericarditis chest pain, not the fluid-overloaded picture of constriction.

C.q: A 74-year-old woman has an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 5.3 cm on computed tomography. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Three-yearly ultrasound is for aneurysms of 3.0 to 3.9 cm. At 5.3 cm a woman has passed her repair threshold of 5.0 cm.
Rupture is a surgical emergency with high risk; the aim of surveillance is to repair before it. At 5.3 cm she meets the threshold for elective repair.
Correct. Elective repair is recommended at 5.0 cm or larger in women (over 5.5 cm in men). Women's aneurysms rupture more often, which is why their threshold is lower.
Surveillance every six to 12 months fits 4.0 to 5.4 cm in men below their threshold. For a woman, 5.0 cm or larger means elective repair.

C.q: A 33-year-old man had a plaster cast removed from his right lower leg two days ago after a tibial fracture. Nothing else on the Wells criteria is present and no alternative diagnosis is as likely. What is his Wells score?
opts: One point undercounts. Each of his three positive items is worth 1 point, and none is offset by a likelier alternative diagnosis, which would subtract 2, so his total is three.
Two points would omit one positive item. The plaster immobilization, the calf swelling over 3 cm and the deep venous tenderness each score 1, so the total is three.

Correct. Recent plaster immobilization of the lower extremity, calf swelling over 3 cm and tenderness along the deep venous system are worth 1 point each, for 3. A score of 3 or more means high likelihood, so ultrasound is ordered.

C.q: A 38-year-old woman has her second recurrence of idiopathic pericarditis despite colchicine. Her temperature is 38.4 degrees Celsius, C-reactive protein is 45 mg/L, and cardiac magnetic resonance shows pericardial edema with late gadolinium enhancement. Which therapy is most appropriate to add?
opts: Correct. With an inflammatory phenotype (C-reactive protein above 10 mg/L, fever, imaging inflammation) and a colchicine-resistant second recurrence of idiopathic disease, an interleukin-1 blocker such as anakinra or rilonacept is added and now used earlier.
Intravenous immunoglobulin is a later-line option on the older treatment table. For colchicine-resistant recurrence with an inflammatory phenotype, anti-interleukin-1 therapy is preferred.

C.q: A 45-year-old man presents with new-onset heart failure a week after a flulike illness. He smokes and has hyperlipidemia, so the team wants to exclude coronary disease before labeling this myocarditis. Which test rules out coronary ischemia as the cause of his new heart failure?
opts: The chest radiograph is nonspecific and may show cardiomegaly, but it cannot show the coronary arteries. Cardiac angiography rules out ischemia.
The erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated in myocarditis but is nonspecific and cannot exclude coronary disease. Angiography does.
Correct. Cardiac angiography is used in the myocarditis work-up to rule out coronary ischemia as the cause of new-onset heart failure, which matters in a patient with coronary risk factors.
Biopsy is the gold standard for confirming myocarditis once other causes are excluded, but it does not image the coronary arteries. Angiography rules out ischemia.

C.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has native valve endocarditis from penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococci. The team is choosing his antibiotic plan. Which choice should be avoided?
opts: Correct. The 2-week regimen with gentamicin is reserved for uncomplicated endocarditis with a rapid response and no chronic kidney disease; gentamicin is nephrotoxic, so he needs a standard course without it.
Close monitoring of labs and renal function is part of endocarditis management, especially with kidney disease.
Penicillin G for the full course
Penicillin G is a standard directed agent for viridans streptococci and is appropriate for him.
Ceftriaxone is a standard directed agent for viridans streptococci and does not depend on gentamicin.

C.q: A 66-year-old man with a large anterior myocardial infarction two years ago has palpitations and lightheadedness. He is alert, with a blood pressure of 112/70. The monitor shows a regular wide QRS rhythm at 170 per minute with no P waves, every complex the same shape, for over a minute. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Ventricular fibrillation is uncoordinated activity with no pulse. He is alert with a blood pressure, and the rhythm is organized.

Correct. A regular wide QRS rhythm of 100 to 250 per minute without P waves, with identical complexes lasting over 30 seconds, is sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, often seen after myocardial infarction.
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia has QRS complexes that vary in shape. Identical complexes make this monomorphic.
Complete block gives a slow wide rhythm, usually below 40, with dissociated P waves. This rhythm is fast at 170.

C.q: A 66-year-old woman with aortic valve endocarditis has a transesophageal echocardiogram that shows an abscess around the valve ring. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Waiting months allows the abscess to destroy tissue around the valve; abscess is an indication for surgery now.
Oral therapy is not appropriate; an abscess calls for surgical evaluation with continued parenteral antibiotics.
An abscess makes the infection complicated; shortening therapy is never appropriate here.

Correct. Abscess is an indication for surgery, alongside heart failure from valve dysfunction, infection not resolving on appropriate antibiotics and fungal infection, so cardiothoracic surgery evaluates her.

C.q: A 58-year-old woman has Wenckebach block (a PR interval that grows longer until a beat is dropped) found on a routine tracing. She feels well and asks what would make her a candidate for a pacemaker. Which answer is most accurate?
opts: Correct. Mobitz type I needs no treatment unless symptoms are debilitating; a permanent pacemaker is considered for symptomatic patients, such as those with dizziness, exertional intolerance or syncope.
Dropped beats are the defining pattern of Mobitz type I, often with increased vagal tone, and need no treatment by themselves. Symptoms are what make her a pacemaker candidate.
A PR interval above 0.20 seconds is part of the lengthening pattern itself, not a pacing indication. In Mobitz type I it is symptoms that make a patient a pacemaker candidate.
Age alone is not an indication. Mobitz type I is usually asymptomatic and needs no treatment; a pacemaker is considered once the block causes symptoms.

C.q: In unstable Mobitz type II block, when medications are not used or do not work, which is the emergent measure?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion treats unstable tachycardias with a pulse. A failing conduction system with a slow rate needs pacing, not a shock.
Vagal maneuvers slow atrioventricular conduction and would worsen a block. The emergent measure is transcutaneous pacing.
Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Unstable Mobitz type II block is paced transcutaneously.
Correct. Transcutaneous pacing, with pads on the chest, is the emergent measure for unstable Mobitz type II block; it bridges the patient to a permanent pacemaker.

C.q: Stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response is treated how?
opts: Correct. A hemodynamically stable patient in rapid ventricular response gets intravenous rate control; a stable patient without it gets rate control by mouth.
Synchronized cardioversion is for the unstable patient; a stable patient in rapid ventricular response is rate-controlled intravenously.
Mapping and ablation is a later, elective rhythm option, not the acute treatment of rapid ventricular response.
Atropine speeds the heart and treats unstable bradycardia; it would worsen rapid ventricular response.

C.q: A 64-year-old man in atrial flutter has a heart rate of 150, a blood pressure of 70/40, and is confused. Which is the next step?
opts: Oral rate control is for the stable patient; hypotension and confusion call for synchronized cardioversion.
Three weeks of anticoagulation precedes elective outpatient cardioversion; an unstable patient is cardioverted now.
Vagal maneuvers are first line for stable supraventricular tachycardia; unstable flutter needs synchronized cardioversion.
Correct. Hemodynamically unstable atrial flutter (hypotension with confusion) is treated with synchronized cardioversion.

C.q: A 71-year-old woman admitted with stress cardiomyopathy after a house fire has a repeat echocardiogram that shows a thrombus in the akinetic left ventricular apex. She is in sinus rhythm. Which treatment is now indicated?
opts: A nitrate infusion does not treat a ventricular thrombus. Supportive care in Takotsubo adds anticoagulation when a left ventricular thrombus is present.
A pacemaker treats heart block from conduction disease, which she does not have. A left ventricular thrombus calls for anticoagulation.

Correct. Treatment of Takotsubo is empiric and supportive and depends on the presentation: anticoagulation if a left ventricular thrombus is present, beta blockers as helpful, and diuretics if heart failure is present.
Myectomy relieves septal obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A thrombus in the akinetic apex is treated with anticoagulation.

C.q: A 26-year-old woman had a peripherally inserted central catheter placed in her right arm two weeks ago for long-term antibiotic therapy. She reports aching and swelling of the arm. Examination shows diffuse swelling of the entire right upper arm with mild redness, and there is no palpable cord and no purulent drainage. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Venous duplex ultrasound of the arm

Correct. Upper extremity deep vein thrombosis often presents only with limb swelling and arm discomfort, and indwelling central venous catheters are a leading cause. Duplex ultrasound of the involved limb is the test.

That plan treats superficial thrombophlebitis, marked by a tender palpable cord along one vein. Swelling of the whole arm after a central catheter raises deep vein thrombosis, which needs imaging first.
Cellulitis involves spreading painful redness, often with fever. Diffuse arm swelling with mild redness after a central catheter is more likely upper extremity deep vein thrombosis and needs imaging.
Elevation alone would risk missing a deep clot. Whole-arm swelling after a central line needs duplex ultrasound, since upper extremity deep vein thrombosis can cause pulmonary embolism.

C.q: A 45-year-old woman with varicose veins has a small, tender, red cord along the great saphenous vein of the calf. Venous duplex ultrasound confirms a short segment of superficial clot. She has no other risk factors for thrombosis. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Filters are reserved for acute proximal lower extremity deep vein thrombosis when anticoagulation fails or is contraindicated. A short superficial clot rarely embolizes and needs symptomatic care.

Antibiotics treat infection within the vein, which brings high fever, purulent drainage or redness well beyond the vein. This sterile inflammation responds to compresses, elevation and anti-inflammatory drugs.

Correct. Typical treatment is warm compresses, compression, elevation of the limb and an anti-inflammatory drug such as ibuprofen or diclofenac for pain and inflammation. Anticoagulation is reserved for higher risk.
Thrombolysis is used for large proximal deep vein thrombosis or a stable pulmonary embolism. A short superficial clot is treated with compresses, compression, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug.

C.q: A 33-year-old man has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 190 with hidden P waves. He is alert with a blood pressure of 128/80. A properly performed vagal maneuver does not change the rhythm. Which is the next step?
opts: Magnesium breaks torsades de pointes; a stable narrow complex tachycardia gets adenosine after a failed vagal maneuver.
Correct. In stable supraventricular tachycardia, adenosine follows a failed vagal maneuver and may be repeated once; it may convert the rhythm or slow it enough to show P waves.
Atropine speeds the heart and treats unstable bradycardia; it would not stop a supraventricular tachycardia.
Synchronized cardioversion is for instability; this stable patient moves from a vagal maneuver to adenosine.

C.q: A 67-year-old woman is recovering in hospital from stress cardiomyopathy that followed news of her son's serious illness. Her chest pain has resolved, and she asks whether her heart will stay damaged. Which answer about her prognosis is most accurate?
opts: Correct. Takotsubo is a transient regional systolic dysfunction, and most patients completely recover, which distinguishes its prognosis from the progressive cardiomyopathies.
The dysfunction in Takotsubo is transient, and most patients recover completely rather than progressing to chronic heart failure.
The poorest prognosis among heart muscle diseases belongs to restrictive cardiomyopathy. Stress cardiomyopathy usually resolves completely.
Fifty percent mortality at five years describes symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy. Most patients with stress cardiomyopathy recover completely.

C.q: A 31-year-old woman has inappropriate sinus tachycardia at about 110 after a full workup excluded other causes. Her only symptom is awareness of her heartbeat, and she asks whether she needs medication. Which response is most accurate?
opts: She needs a lifelong beta blocker
Beta blockers are not well tolerated in inappropriate sinus tachycardia, which is why it is usually left untreated.
Anticoagulation prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation and flutter; a sinus tachycardia carries no such need.

Correct. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is generally left untreated: patients tolerate the symptoms better than the treatment, beta blockers are poorly tolerated, and the prognosis is usually benign.
Cardioversion resets reentrant or fibrillatory rhythms; inappropriate sinus tachycardia is a sinus rhythm and is usually left untreated.

C.q: A 62-year-old woman with suspected tamponade undergoes right heart catheterization before drainage. Which pressure finding is expected?
opts: An isolated high left atrial pressure
An isolated left atrial rise suggests left-sided failure or mitral disease; tamponade equalizes all chambers.
Right-sided pressures are high, not low, in tamponade, matching the distended neck veins.
Correct. Cardiac catheterization in tamponade shows equalization of pressures in all chambers of the heart, because the pericardial fluid under pressure dictates diastolic pressure throughout.
A gradient across the aortic valve
A transvalvular gradient indicates aortic stenosis, not tamponade, which equalizes pressures in all chambers.

C.q: A 76-year-old woman has episodes of lightheadedness and one faint. A 24-hour ambulatory monitor shows runs of a fast, irregular rhythm that alternate with slow rates and long pauses. Which fast rhythm is most likely on her monitor?
opts: Nodal reentry is a regular narrow tachycardia, usually in younger women without heart disease; it is not the fast phase of tachy-brady syndrome.
Correct. Fast rhythms alternating with bradycardia and offset pauses are tachy-brady syndrome, a form of sick sinus syndrome in which the tachyarrhythmia is most commonly atrial fibrillation.
In tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm comes from outside the failing sinus node, most commonly atrial fibrillation.
Ventricular fibrillation is a pulseless arrest rhythm, not a recurring run she survives; the usual fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome is atrial fibrillation.

C.q: Why is renal function checked in peripheral artery disease?
opts: Homocysteine is a blood level, not a kidney function test. Renal function is checked for the risk of renal insufficiency.
Stones are not the concern named. Renal function is checked because these patients are at risk of renal insufficiency.
Claudication is graded by history and the ankle-brachial index. Renal function is checked because of renal insufficiency risk.
Correct. Patients with peripheral artery disease are at risk for renal insufficiency, so renal function joins the electrocardiogram, blood count, lipid profile, metabolic panel and hemoglobin A1c.

C.q: A 72-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has a routine electrocardiogram. The QRS is 0.16 seconds wide, with a dominant S wave in V1, a broad single-peaked R wave in leads I, V5 and V6, and no Q waves in those leads. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A QRS over 0.12 seconds with a dominant S wave in V1, a monophasic R in the lateral leads and absent Q waves in I, V5 and V6 is left bundle branch block; chronic hypertension is a named cause.
Right bundle branch block gives an rsR' pattern in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in I and aVL, not a dominant S in V1.
Ventricular tachycardia is a fast rhythm of 100 to 250 per minute without P waves. A routine tracing with a wide QRS and the lateral pattern is left bundle branch block.
First-degree block lengthens the PR interval with a narrow QRS. A QRS of 0.16 seconds with this lead pattern is left bundle branch block.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
C.q: A 41-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy also has enlarged hilar lymph nodes and skin nodules, and an infiltrative process such as sarcoidosis is suspected. Coronary angiography showed no disease. Which imaging test best identifies an inflammatory or infiltrative cause?
opts: Ambulatory rhythm monitoring for forty-eight hours
Ambulatory monitoring assesses arrhythmia and sudden death risk, most notably in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It cannot show infiltration of the heart muscle.
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium
Correct. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium contrast helps identify inflammatory, ischemic or infiltrative processes such as sarcoidosis or hemochromatosis in dilated cardiomyopathy.
A repeat resting electrocardiogram in six months
Repeating the electrocardiogram adds rhythm and conduction information only. Tissue characterization for sarcoidosis needs cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium.
Pressure tracings are used to evaluate restrictive physiology. Identifying inflammation or infiltration is the job of gadolinium-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance imaging.

C.q: A 24-year-old man whose Wolff-Parkinson-White was found on a school electrocardiogram presents with palpitations. The rhythm is irregular and wide-complex, at rates up to 260, with varying delta waves (slurred upstrokes). He is alert with a blood pressure of 118/74. Which drug is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Correct. Irregular, wide, very fast complexes in a patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White are pre-excited atrial fibrillation, treated with intravenous procainamide; adenosine must never be used.
Atropine speeds conduction and is for unstable bradycardia; it would accelerate a pre-excited tachycardia.
Magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a long QT, not pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
Adenosine is contraindicated here: it blocks only the normal node and lets the accessory pathway carry the fibrillation.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
C.q: A 70-year-old man had 20 minutes of weakness and numbness in his right hand four months ago that fully resolved. Duplex ultrasonography shows 75% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. A friend with no symptoms was told surgery waits until stenosis passes 80%, and he asks whether the same applies to him. Which response is accurate?
opts: Yes; resolved symptoms do not count
A transient ischemic attack lasts under 24 hours by definition, and one within the last six months still makes him symptomatic. Asymptomatic means no stroke or attack in the last six months.

Correct. A transient ischemic attack (focal loss of neurologic function lasting under 24 hours) within the last six months makes him symptomatic, and surgery is advised for symptomatic stenosis over 70%; the over-80% rule is for asymptomatic patients.

Over 80%, with a life expectancy over 5 years, is the surgical threshold for asymptomatic stenosis like his friend's. His attack within six months makes him symptomatic, so over 70% applies and 75% qualifies.
No; he needs medical therapy only
Medical management alone is advised for low-grade stenosis under 50%. At 75% with a transient ischemic attack four months ago, he meets the over-70% threshold for surgery in symptomatic patients.

C.q: A 50-year-old man with acute pericarditis says the pain keeps him awake because it is worse when he lies down. Which advice is most appropriate?
opts: Keep the head of the bed elevated
Correct. Pericardial pain is worse supine and better leaning forward, so keeping the head of the bed elevated is advised, along with completing the full treatment course.
Sleep prone to splint the chest
Prone sleeping is not recommended. Elevating the head of the bed eases positional pericardial pain.
Sleep flat to rest the heart
Lying flat is exactly what worsens his pain. The head of the bed should be raised.
Take an extra dose at bedtime
Extra bedtime medication does not address positional pain; elevating the head of the bed eases it.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
C.q: Where do atherosclerotic lesions most often form?
opts: In the smallest arterioles of the skin
Atherosclerosis affects intermediate and large arteries such as the coronary, carotid and femoral arteries and the aorta, not the skin's smallest arterioles.
In straight segments with laminar flow
Laminar flow along straight segments is the protected pattern. Lesions favor bifurcations and turbulent regions, where flow swirls against the wall.
In the veins draining the lower legs
Atherosclerosis is an arterial disease of intermediate and large arteries. It forms at arterial branch points and sites of turbulence, not in leg veins.
At branch points and turbulent sites

Correct. Atherosclerotic lesions form at arterial bifurcations (branching) and at sites of increased turbulence, and they develop over many decades before causing stenosis, thrombosis or atheroemboli.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
C.q: When are palliative care discussions raised for elderly patients with cardiomyopathy?
opts: Palliative discussions are placed in the advanced stages rather than at the first encounter, once the disease has progressed.
They are explicitly part of elderly care. Palliative care discussions are held in the advanced stages of disease.
Transplant is a curative-intent option in advanced adult disease; palliative discussions in the elderly come in advanced stages, not after transplant.
Correct. Palliative care discussions belong to the advanced stages in the elderly, alongside tailored therapy, cautious diuretics and vasodilators, and a focus on quality of life.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
C.q: A 76-year-old woman has constant throbbing, burning pain in her toes and forefoot that is worse lying flat, not relieved by narcotic pain medicine, and eased by dangling her leg or walking around. Her feet are cool. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Claudication is activity-related muscle pain relieved by rest, usually in about 10 minutes. Her pain is constant and eased by walking or dangling, which is ischemic rest pain.

Peripheral neuropathy gives a continuous burning sensation in the foot that is unaffected by exercise. Her pain changes with position, worse lying flat and eased by dangling, which is arterial rest pain.

Acute limb ischemia is a sudden occlusion with abrupt onset of severe pain and absent pulses. Her constant pain that worsens lying flat and eases with dangling is the pattern of critical limb ischemia.

Correct. Ischemic rest pain of critical limb ischemia is constant, distal, worse with elevation or reclining, poorly controlled even by narcotics, and relieved by dependency or walking, which use gravity to aid perfusion.

C.q: Which acute event can cause right bundle branch block by suddenly raising right ventricular pressure?
opts: A hypertensive crisis raises left ventricular afterload. The acute right ventricular pressure load named is pulmonary embolism.
Aortic dissection loads the left side and the aorta, not the right ventricle. Pulmonary embolism is the acute cause named.
Correct. A sudden increase in right ventricular pressure, as from a pulmonary embolism, is a named cause of right bundle branch block.
Gastroenteritis does not load the right ventricle. A pulmonary embolism suddenly raises right ventricular pressure and can cause the block.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
C.q: A 69-year-old woman with right-sided heart failure, ascites and a raised jugular venous pressure has cardiac magnetic resonance imaging to decide between restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive pericarditis. Which imaging finding would point to constrictive pericarditis instead?
opts: A preserved ejection fraction until late stages is typical of restrictive cardiomyopathy, so it does not separate it from constriction. A thickened pericardium is the finding that points toward constriction.
A normal or near-normal cavity size is expected in restrictive cardiomyopathy. The finding that points to constrictive pericarditis is pericardial thickening.

Correct. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging helps separate the two conditions, and a thickened pericardium points to constrictive pericarditis rather than restrictive cardiomyopathy, though constriction can occur with a normal-thickness pericardium.
Marked enlargement of one or both atria is a feature of restrictive cardiomyopathy itself, caused by impaired ventricular filling. It does not point to pericarditis.

C.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
C.q: A 58-year-old woman with previous infective endocarditis needs a root canal. She developed hives (urticaria) after amoxicillin years ago and can take pills. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Amoxicillin is a penicillin and caused her hives, so it is avoided; a macrolide such as azithromycin is used instead.
ruled out by a stated finding
Cephalosporins should not be used after anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria with penicillin, and she had hives.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. A penicillin-allergic patient who can take oral medication gets azithromycin or clarithromycin, or doxycycline; cephalexin is avoided after urticaria to penicillin.
Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.

C.q: A 66-year-old woman in torsades de pointes (a polymorphic rhythm whose QRS complexes twist around the baseline) becomes unresponsive with a blood pressure of 60/30 and only a faint pulse. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. A hemodynamically unstable patient in torsades de pointes is defibrillated (unsynchronized cardioversion); polymorphic rhythms are not synchronized.
Lidocaine may be used in the stable patient. Instability calls for defibrillation.
Pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms with a pulse. Unstable torsades needs defibrillation.
A polymorphic rhythm has no consistent QRS to synchronize to. Unstable torsades is defibrillated.

C.q: A 68-year-old man has had 6 weeks of low-grade fever and weight loss and has a new murmur. Subacute endocarditis is suspected. Which complete blood count finding is most likely?
opts: Eosinophilia points to allergy or parasites, not endocarditis; expect leukocytosis with a normocytic anemia of chronic disease.
Correct. The complete blood count often shows leukocytosis and anemia of chronic disease with a normal mean corpuscular volume (normocytic).
Small red cells suggest iron deficiency, not the anemia of chronic disease, which is normocytic.
Chronic infection lowers, not raises, the red cell mass; expect a normocytic anemia.

C.q: A 65-year-old woman with a normal pulse examination and ankle-brachial index has had her venous ulcer heal after months of compression. She asks why it opened again after she bumped her leg. Which feature of a healed venous ulcer explains this?
opts: Correct. A venous ulcer heals with a thin scar that breaks down easily with minor trauma or increased leg edema, so recurrence is common without consistent compression.
A closed ulcer without signs of infection does not explain new breakdown. The healed area is a thin scar that opens with trauma or increased edema.
Lymphatic obstruction causes lymphedema, a different disorder. A healed venous ulcer reopens because its scar is thin and fragile.
Her pulses and ankle-brachial index are normal, so arterial supply is adequate. The scar itself is thin and breaks down with minor trauma or recurrent edema.

C.q: A 30-year-old woman with known atrioventricular nodal reentry has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 178. She is stable. Which treatment almost always terminates it?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is rarely required in nodal reentry and is kept for the unstable patient.
Ablation offers a definitive cure for selected patients but is not how an acute episode is stopped.
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, not nodal reentry.
Correct. Atrioventricular nodal reentry almost always terminates with vagal maneuvers or adenosine; synchronized cardioversion is rarely required.

C.q: A 54-year-old man has a moderate-to-large pericardial effusion on echocardiogram with no hemodynamic compromise. Viral, uremic, thyroid and rheumatologic workups are unrevealing. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Anti-interleukin-1 therapy is for recurrent inflammatory pericarditis, not an undiagnosed effusion.
Pericardiectomy or a window is for recurrent or loculated effusions. First the cause should be found by sampling the fluid.

Correct. Diagnostic pericardiocentesis is considered for a moderate-to-large effusion of unknown etiology, as well as during therapeutic drainage for tamponade and with suspected neoplastic, purulent or tuberculous disease.
An unexplained moderate-to-large effusion needs a diagnosis; the fluid should be sampled rather than ignored.

C.q: A 72-year-old man with extensive atherosclerosis develops painful, tender, bluish discoloration of several toes on his left foot, with localized pallor. His dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are easily palpable. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Atheroemboli of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from proximal plaques lodge in small vessels of muscle and skin, causing blue toe syndrome with tenderness and pallor while distal pulses usually stay palpable.
A thromboembolus occluding a limb artery produces a cold, pale leg with absent pulses. Palpable pulses with painful blue toes point to atheroembolism.
Dry gangrene is hard, black, mummified tissue with clear demarcation. Tender blue toes with palpable pulses reflect small-vessel atheroemboli.
Critical limb ischemia is chronic rest pain and tissue loss with diminished pulses. Sudden painful blue toes with easily palpable pulses is atheroembolism.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
C.q: A 23-year-old previously healthy man has breathlessness, chest pain and exercise intolerance ten days after a flulike illness with fever, myalgia and diarrhea. He is tachycardic with a third heart sound (an early diastolic sound just after the second heart sound) and crackles at both bases. Troponin is elevated and coronary angiography is normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy follows an emotional or physical stressor, and 90% of cases are postmenopausal women. A viral prodrome in a young man points to myocarditis.

Correct. Acute heart failure in an otherwise healthy young man with no cardiac history, one to two weeks after a flulike prodrome, with raised troponin and normal coronaries, is acute viral myocarditis.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy is rare, presents late with right-sided congestion, and follows infiltration, radiation or chemotherapy rather than a recent viral illness.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an inherited thickening of the septum with an outflow murmur and exertional syncope, not acute heart failure after a viral illness.

C.q: A 71-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted with an exacerbation and respiratory failure. His pulse is 128 and irregular. The electrocardiogram shows a P wave before every QRS, with at least three different P-wave shapes in lead II. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves at all; his rhythm has a P wave before every QRS, in three shapes.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. An irregular tachycardia with a P wave for every QRS and at least three distinct P-wave shapes in one lead is multifocal atrial tachycardia, usually from severe lung disease or heart failure in an acutely ill patient.
Flutter shows uniform sawtooth waves at 250 or more; his discrete P waves in three different shapes point to multifocal atrial tachycardia.
Focal atrial tachycardia is regular, with one consistent abnormal P wave from a single focus, not three shapes.
ruled out by a stated finding

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
C.q: A 28-year-old woman with a malar rash, painful joints and a positive antinuclear antibody test has a new murmur. She has no fever, repeated blood cultures are negative, and echocardiography shows small sterile-appearing valve vegetations. Which is the most likely cause of her valve lesion?
opts: Without fever and with repeatedly negative cultures, a lupus patient's valve lesion is far more likely non-infective Libman-Sacks endocarditis.
ruled out by a stated finding
No pacemaker or defibrillator is described; her lupus, absent fever and negative cultures point to a non-infective valve lesion.
Acute endocarditis is hectically febrile and toxic with positive cultures, which she lacks.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. Systemic lupus erythematosus may present with non-infective (Libman-Sacks) endocarditis, which mimics infective endocarditis in the autoimmune differential.

C.q: A 57-year-old woman in ventricular fibrillation arrest has received shocks, epinephrine and amiodarone, and she remains in ventricular fibrillation. Which drug may be considered next?
opts: Metoprolol is not the next step in refractory arrest. Lidocaine may be considered.
Adenosine is for narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia. Lidocaine is considered here.
Correct. Lidocaine is considered for ventricular fibrillation that remains refractory to shocks after amiodarone.
Verapamil is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker for atrial rhythms. Lidocaine may be considered in shock-refractory arrest.

C.q: A 66-year-old man with a known ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm develops a new diastolic murmur, exertional dyspnea and leg swelling. Which complication does the aneurysm's location explain?
opts: Esophageal compression with dysphagia is a descending aneurysm effect. An ascending aneurysm produces aortic regurgitation and heart failure.
Correct. An ascending thoracic aneurysm can cause aortic regurgitation and heart failure, which explains the new diastolic murmur, breathlessness and edema.
Tracheal compression with stridor and wheeze comes from a descending aneurysm. The ascending location explains aortic regurgitation.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement, with hoarseness, comes from an arch aneurysm. The ascending aorta causes aortic regurgitation and heart failure.

C.q: In the low likelihood Wells category, what happens after a negative D-dimer?
opts: Ultrasound follows a positive D-dimer, not a negative one. A negative result in the low likelihood category ends the work-up.
Venography is invasive and largely replaced by ultrasound. A negative D-dimer in the low category ends the work-up.
The test is repeated in a week
Repeat imaging applies after a negative ultrasound in high likelihood patients. A negative D-dimer in the low category ends the work-up.
Correct. In the low likelihood Wells category a negative D-dimer ends the work-up, since the test is sensitive enough to rule out deep vein thrombosis.

C.q: A 52-year-old man with a pacemaker implanted two weeks ago has three days of swelling and aching of the left arm. The pacemaker lead has injured the wall of the subclavian vein. Which component of the Virchow triad does this injury represent?
opts: A hypercoagulable state is a clotting tendency from inherited disorders, cancer, estrogen or pregnancy. Mechanical injury to the vein wall from a lead is endothelial trauma instead.

Correct. Damage to the vessel lining from an indwelling device is endothelial trauma, one leg of the Virchow triad. Pacemakers, implanted defibrillators and central venous catheters are the most common causes of upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis.
Venous stasis arises from immobilization, heart failure or venous insufficiency. A lead scraping the vein wall is physical injury to the lining, which is the endothelial trauma component.
Impaired lymphatic drainage causes lymphedema and is not part of the Virchow triad. Injury to the subclavian vein wall is endothelial trauma, the third triad component.

C.q: A 37-year-old man was treated for acute pericarditis 4 weeks ago and now feels well. A repeat electrocardiogram shows widespread T-wave inversions without ST elevation, and troponin is normal. Which best explains the tracing?
opts: Correct. The classic evolution is widespread ST elevation with PR depression, then ST normalization with T-wave flattening, then inversion of the flattened T waves, and finally a normal tracing.
With normal troponin and a known recent pericarditis, diffuse T-wave inversion fits the third stage of the pericarditis evolution.
ruled out by a stated finding
Tamponade gives low voltage and electrical alternans with hemodynamic signs, not isolated T-wave inversion in a well patient.
Hyperkalemia peaks the T waves rather than inverting them; this is the expected evolution of pericarditis.

C.q: A 71-year-old man admitted with pneumonia develops frequent early, wide QRS beats with no preceding P wave on telemetry, and he feels his heart skipping. His oxygen saturation on the monitor is drifting down. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Amiodarone is for ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation. Premature beats are addressed by finding and correcting hypoxemia or electrolytes.
Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. He has isolated premature beats with a pulse.
Ablation is reserved for refractory symptoms or beat-induced cardiomyopathy. The first step is to correct hypoxemia and electrolytes.
Correct. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance are the main causes of premature ventricular contractions, so new frequent beats call for checking oxygenation and electrolytes first.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. C.q: An 80-year-old man is found on the floor two days after collapsing. His right leg has profound sensory loss, paralysis with rigid muscles, and no arterial or venous Doppler signal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Imaging suits viable and marginally threatened limbs. For an irreversibly damaged limb, vascular imaging is generally not immediately needed; the limb requires amputation.
Thrombolysis can restore flow to a salvageable limb of under 14 days. This limb is irreversibly damaged, and major amputation is needed regardless of therapy.
Clot removal is for limbs that can still be saved. Profound sensory loss, paralysis and absent venous signals mark an irreversible limb that needs major amputation.

Correct. An irreversibly ischemic limb has major tissue loss or permanent nerve damage, profound sensory loss, paralysis and inaudible arterial and venous signals; nonviable limbs require major amputation whatever therapy is used.

C.q: What is the first-line treatment for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is definitive care for chronic symptomatic bradycardia; the acute, unstable patient first gets atropine, then a temporary pacemaker.
Adenosine slows conduction through the atrioventricular node and is used for stable supraventricular tachycardia; it would worsen a bradycardia.
Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, not a drug to speed a slow heart; atropine is first line.
Correct. Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia; if it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows, and chronic symptomatic disease gets a permanent pacemaker.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
C.q: A 49-year-old man has a first proximal deep vein thrombosis with no surgery, trauma, hormone use, travel, cancer or other identifiable trigger, and no inherited disorder has been found. How long should anticoagulation continue?
opts: Three to six months fits a clot provoked by a minor transient factor such as estrogen therapy, pregnancy, minor surgery or travel. An unprovoked clot has no such trigger and needs longer therapy.

Correct. A first venous thromboembolism with no identifiable risk factor is unprovoked, and its source, such as an undiscovered inherited clotting disorder, is unknown. Treatment therefore continues for an indefinite length of time.
Six weeks is shorter than the minimum of three months required after any first venous thromboembolism. An unprovoked clot needs indefinite therapy.
Three months is the minimum for a clot provoked by a major transient risk factor such as surgery or major trauma. An unprovoked clot has no reversible trigger, so treatment continues beyond it.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 21-year-old man has mild breathlessness and fatigue two weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection. Troponin is mildly raised, echocardiogram shows mildly reduced function, and he is hemodynamically stable. Which is the mainstay of his treatment?
opts: Correct. Treatment of myocarditis is directed toward the clinical scenario, and supportive care is the mainstay, with vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, diuretics, antiarrhythmics or anticoagulation as needed.
Alcohol septal ablation treats outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Myocarditis is treated with supportive care directed at the clinical scenario.
Biopsy is reserved for acute deterioration of unknown origin not responding to treatment. A stable patient with mild symptoms is managed with supportive care.
Most patients with mild symptoms recover completely, so transplant listing has no place here. Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: A 53-year-old man has had positive blood cultures for 10 days despite an antibiotic regimen that matches his organism's sensitivities, and he still has fevers. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. Infection not resolving with appropriate antibiotic therapy is an indication for surgery, as are heart failure from valve dysfunction, abscess and fungal infection.
Stopping therapy in persistent bacteremia risks valve destruction and death; surgical evaluation is indicated instead.
Anticoagulation is not beneficial in native valve infection and does not clear bacteremia.
Oral step-down does not treat persistent bacteremia; therapy stays parenteral, and infection not resolving on appropriate antibiotics is a surgical indication.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: A 77-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve has endocarditis, and his blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. His son asks how serious this organism is. Which statement is most accurate?
opts: A relatively good prognosis belongs to viridans streptococci treated before complications, not Staphylococcus aureus.
Prosthetic valve staphylococcal infection is severe; surgery is evaluated by cardiothoracic surgery when indicated.
Therapy alone runs weeks (typically 4-6 from the first negative culture), and the infection is the most lethal kind.
It is the most lethal cause
Correct. Staphylococcus aureus is the most lethal organism in endocarditis, with mortality highest in prosthetic valve endocarditis (about 50%).

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 46-year-old man with frothy urine and leg swelling is found to have a moderate pericardial effusion. Which tests best evaluate the suspected cause?
opts: A urine culture looks for a urinary infection, which frothy urine does not suggest; frothy urine with edema points to nephrotic syndrome, so albumin and urine protein are checked.
Thyroid tests look for myxedema; his frothy urine and edema point to nephrotic syndrome.
Correct. Albumin and urine protein screen for nephrotic syndrome as a cause of pericardial effusion, alongside thyroid, rheumatologic, infectious and malignancy evaluation.
An antinuclear antibody looks for lupus. His picture fits nephrotic syndrome, tested with albumin and urine protein.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 68-year-old man with dilated non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, an ejection fraction of 25% and breathlessness on minimal exertion despite optimal medical therapy has a left bundle branch block with a QRS of 0.16 seconds. Which treatment addresses the conduction problem?
opts: Magnesium treats torsades de pointes. Symptomatic left bundle branch block with reduced ejection fraction is treated with a biventricular pacer.
Correct. Left bundle branch block is usually left untreated, except symptomatic left bundle branch block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, which gets a biventricular pacer.
A conventional pacemaker treats slow rhythms. Resynchronizing the ventricles in this setting calls for a biventricular pacer.
Ablation destroys tissue and cannot restore left ventricular activation. A biventricular pacer resynchronizes the ventricles.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 58-year-old woman five days after hip replacement develops sudden breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain and a heart rate of 118. Her electrocardiogram shows a new right bundle branch block. Which acute cause of the block should be suspected?
opts: An effusion lowers voltage and can cause tamponade, but it is not the named acute cause of right bundle branch block. Pulmonary embolism is.
A hypertensive crisis loads the left ventricle. A sudden right ventricular pressure rise from pulmonary embolism fits.
Aortic dissection causes tearing chest or back pain and loads the aorta, not the right ventricle. Pulmonary embolism fits her picture.
Correct. A sudden increase in right ventricular pressure, as from a pulmonary embolism, is a named cause of right bundle branch block, and her postoperative setting fits.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: Which pair of drugs can cause pericarditis through drug-induced lupus?
opts: Metoprolol and lisinopril are not listed causes of pericarditis. The drug-induced lupus pair is procainamide and hydralazine.
Colchicine and ibuprofen treat acute pericarditis as first-line anti-inflammatory therapy. Procainamide and hydralazine cause it through drug-induced lupus.
These antibiotics are not named causes of pericardial disease. Drug-induced lupus pericarditis comes from procainamide and hydralazine.
Correct. Iatrogenic causes include trauma, radiation therapy and drug-induced lupus from procainamide and hydralazine, which can produce both pericarditis and pericardial effusion.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: A 71-year-old man with a permanent pacemaker has severe claudication, and an intervention is planned. Which imaging study should be avoided?
opts: Computed tomography angiography is limited by contrast allergy and decreased renal function, not by a pacemaker. It is usable here if his kidneys and allergy history allow.
Duplex ultrasound uses sound waves with no contrast or radiation and is safe with a pacemaker. It remains the mainstay initial noninvasive imaging for suspected stenosis.
Correct. Magnetic resonance angiography is contraindicated with pacemakers and intracranial aneurysm clips. It is otherwise the alternative to computed tomography angiography in contrast allergy.
Conventional angiography is the invasive gold standard used to guide a planned intervention. A pacemaker does not prevent it; the pacemaker rules out magnetic resonance.

D.q: A 64-year-old woman has an asymptomatic ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm that now measures 5.9 cm. Repair is planned. Which approach is usually required for this location?
opts: Three-to-five-yearly imaging is for aneurysms under 4.5 cm. At 5.9 cm in the ascending aorta she has passed the 5.5 cm threshold.
Endovascular repair is an option for descending thoracic aneurysms. The ascending aorta usually needs open surgery with aortic root replacement.
The ascending threshold is 5.5 cm (6.0 cm is for descending). At 5.9 cm, repair is indicated, usually open with root replacement.
Correct. Surgery is generally indicated for ascending aneurysms over 5.5 cm, and an ascending aneurysm often requires an open surgical approach with aortic root replacement.

D.q: A 57-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy returns with recurring ankle edema and increasing abdominal girth. She admits to eating canned soups and fast food most days. Which dietary counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Drink extra fluids with every meal
Extra fluid adds to the congestion behind her edema. The dietary point taught for dilated cardiomyopathy is restricting sodium to under two grams a day.
Restrict sodium to under two grams a day
Correct. Patient education for dilated cardiomyopathy includes sodium restriction to less than two grams a day, along with the medication regimen, follow-up and removing any offending source.
Raise salt intake to protect pressure
Extra salt worsens sodium and water retention and the edema she already has. Education for dilated cardiomyopathy is sodium restriction below two grams a day.
No diet change is needed with drugs
Medication does not replace dietary control. Sodium restriction below two grams a day sits alongside the drug regimen in dilated cardiomyopathy education.

D.q: A 27-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is examined by a student who hears a loud systolic murmur at the left sternal border. Respiration does not change it. Which bedside maneuver would soften her murmur?
opts: Standing decreases preload, which worsens outflow obstruction and makes the murmur of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy louder rather than softer.

Correct. Anything that increases blood flow in the heart reduces outflow obstruction and softens the murmur. Handgrip raises afterload, and squatting or passive leg raising raise preload, so all three decrease the murmur.
The Valsalva maneuver decreases preload and increases the outflow obstruction, so it makes the murmur louder. Handgrip, squatting and leg raising soften it.
Amyl nitrite decreases afterload, which increases outflow obstruction and makes the murmur louder. Increasing afterload with handgrip softens it.

opts: Atropine speeds the heart and is for unstable bradycardia; it would worsen rapid ventricular response.
Correct. A hemodynamically stable patient in atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response gets intravenous rate control; rate control is the first goal.
Mapping and ablation is a later, elective rhythm option, not the first treatment of rapid ventricular response.
Synchronized cardioversion is for the hemodynamically unstable patient; she is alert with a normal blood pressure.

D.q: What may the electrocardiogram show in aortic dissection?
opts: Low voltage is not described for dissection. The electrocardiogram may be normal.
ST elevation is not described as a feature of dissection. The electrocardiogram may be entirely normal.
Q waves are not described. A normal electrocardiogram does not exclude dissection.

Correct. The electrocardiogram may be normal in aortic dissection, so the diagnosis rests on computed tomography of the chest and abdomen, magnetic resonance imaging or transesophageal echocardiography.

D.q: A 79-year-old man with multiple serious medical conditions is a poor surgical candidate. He had a transient ischemic attack and has a 90% symptomatic carotid stenosis. Which intervention is most appropriate?
opts: Medical management alone is advised for stenosis under 50%. A symptomatic 90% stenosis warrants revascularization, here by stenting because surgery is high risk.
Correct. Carotid angioplasty with stenting, most often through the common femoral artery, is less invasive and allows intervention in poor surgical candidates with a qualifying stenosis.
Endarterectomy is the gold standard for high-grade stenosis but requires open surgery. For a poor surgical candidate, the less invasive stenting approach is chosen.
Angiography guides an intervention but does not treat the stenosis. A poor surgical candidate with this stenosis is treated with carotid stenting.
